    New to this? Start here

    You should be comfortable with Algebra 2: linear and quadratic functions, factoring, and right-triangle trig. Everything else is built here, one idea at a time.

    How to use a module

    1. Read The idea: the concept in everyday words.
    2. Play with the graph. Drag the points and move the sliders; the numbers underneath update as you go.
    3. Do Try this: guess first, then press Set it up for me and check.
    4. Work the Worked example one step at a time.
    5. Answer Check yourself, then do the practice problems.

    Look for dotted words: tap them for a quick definition. Every simulation has a Coach that explains whatever control you just moved, and a Reset button.

    Four ideas you'll use everywhere

    • Watch how the output changes as the input changes. Adding the same amount is linear, multiplying by the same factor is exponential, repeating is periodic.
    • Rate of change is a slope. The average rate of change between two points is the slope of the line through them.
    • Every function has a family. a·f(b(x − h)) + k stretches and shifts any graph the same way.
    • Inverses undo. Logs undo exponentials, arcsin undoes sin, and the graphs are mirror images across y = x.

    Suggested path

    Following a class: go unit by unit; each module lists its AP unit.

    Before an exam: drill Which tool?, build a mixed set in Exam review, and clear your mistakes queue.

    Free response: try the original questions in FRQ practice.

    Need a number or an equation? Open the Reference button at the bottom right: functions, exponent and log rules, trig values, identities and polar.

    AP Unit 1On the AP examCED 1.1CED 1.2

    Change in tandem & rates of change

    Two quantities that change together tell a story. The average rate of change measures how fast one changes compared with the other.

    The idea

    A function pairs each input with an output, so when the input changes, the output changes in tandem. As x increases, f is increasing if its outputs go up, and decreasing if they go down. How it goes up matters too: if the output rises faster and faster, the graph is concave up; if it rises more and more slowly, concave down.

    The average rate of change of f on [a, b] is the change in output divided by the change in input: (f(b) − f(a)) / (b − a). It is the slope of the secant line through (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)), and it has units: output units per input unit, such as cm per second.

    The rate of change at a point is what the average rates approach as the interval around that point shrinks. You can estimate it with a small interval. A positive rate means increasing; a negative rate means decreasing; a rate that is itself increasing means concave up.

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose Cylinder and press Play. How does the height graph look, and why?

      What you should see

      A straight line: every second adds the same volume to the same-width column, so the height rises by the same amount each second. A constant rate of change.

    2. Choose Cone, point down. When is the water rising fastest?

      What you should see

      At the start, where the glass is narrowest. As it widens, the same volume makes a thinner layer: the height keeps increasing, but at a decreasing rate. The graph is concave down.

    3. Choose Round flask and Play. Where does the graph switch from concave down to concave up?

      What you should see

      At the widest part of the ball, halfway up. Below it the glass widens (rate falling, concave down); above it the glass narrows (rate rising, concave up). That switch is a point of inflection.

    4. In the second lab choose Cyclist with a = 2, b = 4, then press Shrink. What number does the average rate approach?

      What you should see

      From 5 m/s on [2, 4] down toward 4 m/s: the rate at t = 2, the cyclist's speed at that instant.

    5. Choose Cooling coffee. Is the average rate positive or negative? What does it mean?

      What you should see

      Negative, in degrees per minute: the temperature is decreasing. The rates get closer to 0 later on: it cools more and more slowly (decreasing, concave up).

    Worked example: filling a cone-shaped glass

    Water flows at a steady rate into a cone-shaped glass, point down. The table gives the water height h (cm) at time t (s). Find the average rate of change of h on each 10-second interval, and describe how h changes.

    Water height
    t (s)010203040
    h (cm)0.0012.4115.6317.8919.69

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Formula. On [a, b]: (h(b) − h(a)) / (b − a), in cm per second.
    2. [0, 10]. (12.41 − 0)/10 ≈ 1.24 cm/s.
    3. The rest. (15.63 − 12.41)/10 ≈ 0.32, (17.89 − 15.63)/10 ≈ 0.23, (19.69 − 17.89)/10 ≈ 0.18 cm/s.
    4. Describe it. All the rates are positive, so h is increasing. They get smaller, so it rises more and more slowly: the graph is concave down. That fits the glass: it gets wider as it fills.

    Worked example 2: speed from position

    A cyclist starts from a light and has gone d(t) = 0.5t² + 2t meters after t seconds. Find the average speed on [2, 4], [2, 3] and [2, 2.1], and estimate the speed at t = 2.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Values. d(2) = 2 + 4 = 6, d(4) = 8 + 8 = 16, d(3) = 4.5 + 6 = 10.5, d(2.1) = 2.205 + 4.2 = 6.405.
    2. [2, 4]. (16 − 6)/2 = 5 m/s.
    3. [2, 3]. (10.5 − 6)/1 = 4.5 m/s. [2, 2.1]. (6.405 − 6)/0.1 = 4.05 m/s.
    4. Estimate. As the interval shrinks, the average rates approach 4 m/s: the cyclist's speed at t = 2 (what a speedometer would show).

    Common mistakes

    • Dividing by the change in output instead of the change in input.
    • Leaving off units: an average rate of change is "output units per input unit".
    • Confusing decreasing with concave down: a graph can increase and be concave down at the same time.
    • Thinking one average rate describes the whole interval: on [0, 40] the glass averages 0.49 cm/s, but it was much faster at the start.

    Why the secant slope is the average

    If you replaced the actual change by steady change at the average rate, you would end at exactly the same place: f(a) + (average rate)(b − a) = f(b). That straight-line trip is the secant line. A car that drives 150 km in 2 hours has an average rate of 75 km/h, even if it stopped for lunch.

    Check yourself: f(1) = 4 and f(5) = −8. What is the average rate of change of f on [1, 5]?

    Check yourself: On an interval, the average rates of change of g over consecutive equal-length pieces are 6, 4, 3, 1. Which describes g there?

    AP Unit 1On the AP examCED 1.3

    Linear vs quadratic change

    Linear functions change by the same amount every step. Quadratics change by an amount that itself changes steadily.

    The idea

    Take equal steps in the input. For a linear function the output changes by the same amount each step: the average rate of change is constant, and it is the slope. Equal inputs steps, equal output steps.

    For a quadratic function the output changes are not equal, but they change by the same amount each time: the second differences are constant. Over consecutive equal-length intervals, the average rates of change form a linear pattern. For f(x) = ax² + bx + c and steps of size h, the second difference is 2ah².

    That links rates to shape. If the average rates are increasing, the graph bends up (concave up, a > 0); if they are decreasing, it bends down (concave down, a < 0). A line has no bend at all.

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Set a = 0. What do the bars look like, and why?

      What you should see

      All the same height: with a = 0 the function is linear, f(x) = 2x + 1, and every step of 1 in x adds exactly 2.

    2. Set a = 0.5, b = −1, h = 1. How much does each bar grow by?

      What you should see

      By 1 each time: the first differences are −0.5, 0.5, 1.5, 2.5, …, and the second differences are all 2ah² = 2(0.5)(1) = 1.

    3. Keep a = 0.5 and change the step to h = 2. What happens to the second difference?

      What you should see

      It becomes 2(0.5)(2²) = 4: four times as big. It is still constant, so the test still says quadratic.

    4. In the second lab choose Dropped stone. What is the pattern in the average rates?

      What you should see

      They rise by 9.8 m/s every second: the rates lie on a straight line with slope 9.8, the acceleration of gravity. Constant change in the rate is the signature of a quadratic.

    5. Choose Taxi fare. What does the bottom graph show?

      What you should see

      A flat line: every kilometer costs the same, so the rate never changes. Linear.

    Worked example: which kind of function?

    Decide whether the data are linear, quadratic or neither, and find a formula.

    x01234
    f(x)35112135

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. First differences. 5 − 3 = 2, 11 − 5 = 6, 21 − 11 = 10, 35 − 21 = 14. Not constant, so not linear.
    2. Second differences. 6 − 2 = 4, 10 − 6 = 4, 14 − 10 = 4: constant, so quadratic.
    3. Find a. With step 1 the second difference is 2a, so 2a = 4 and a = 2. Then f(0) = c = 3, and f(1) = 2 + b + 3 = 5 gives b = 0.
    4. Formula. f(x) = 2x² + 3. Check: f(4) = 32 + 3 = 35 ✓.

    Worked example 2: a dropped stone

    A stone dropped from a cliff has fallen d(t) = 4.9t² meters after t seconds. Find the average speed in each of the first four seconds. What pattern do you see?

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Distances. d(0) = 0, d(1) = 4.9, d(2) = 19.6, d(3) = 44.1, d(4) = 78.4 m.
    2. Average speeds. 4.9, 14.7, 24.5 and 34.3 m/s on [0, 1], [1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 4].
    3. Pattern. Each average speed is 9.8 m/s more than the one before. The rates change at a constant rate, which is exactly what makes d quadratic (second difference 2ah² = 2(4.9)(1) = 9.8).
    4. Meaning. 9.8 m/s per second is the acceleration of gravity. The rates are increasing, so the graph of d is concave up.

    Common mistakes

    • Testing differences when the x-values are not equally spaced.
    • Stopping at the first differences: unequal first differences rule out linear but do not prove quadratic.
    • Using the second difference as a: with step 1 it is 2a, not a.
    • Calling a function concave up because it is increasing.

    Where 2ah² comes from

    For f(x) = ax² + bx + c, the change over [x, x + h] is f(x + h) − f(x) = 2ahx + ah² + bh. That is a linear function of x with slope 2ah, so moving x forward by h changes it by 2ah · h = 2ah². The b and c terms only shift the first differences; they never affect the second ones.

    Check yourself: A table has x = 0, 1, 2, 3 and y = 7, 4, 1, −2. The function is

    Check yourself: The second differences of a quadratic with step 1 are all −6. What is a?

    AP Unit 1On the AP examCED 1.4

    Polynomial functions

    A polynomial can turn around only a limited number of times. Where it turns, and where its bending switches, tells you the shape.

    The idea

    A polynomial of degree n is f(x) = aₙxⁿ + … + a₁x + a₀ with aₙ ≠ 0. Its graph is smooth and unbroken. Where f switches from increasing to decreasing it has a relative (local) maximum; where it switches from decreasing to increasing, a relative minimum. Together these are the relative extrema, and a polynomial of degree n has at most n − 1 of them.

    On an interval, the greatest output is the absolute (global) maximum and the least is the absolute minimum. Look at the relative extrema inside the interval and at the two endpoints: the largest and smallest of those values win. An endpoint can beat every turning point.

    A point of inflection is where the graph switches concavity: where the rate of change switches from increasing to decreasing, or the other way. Between two real zeros of a polynomial there is always at least one relative extremum.

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose Cubic. Drag the points until the graph has no turning points at all. Can you make three?

      What you should see

      No turning points is easy (put the points in rising order along a gentle curve). Three is impossible: a cubic has at most 3 − 1 = 2.

    2. With the cubic, where is the gold inflection point compared with the two orange turning points?

      What you should see

      Exactly halfway between them (in x). Every cubic is symmetric about its inflection point.

    3. Choose Quartic. Find a stretch where the top band is green (increasing) and the bottom band says ∩ (concave down). What is the graph doing there?

      What you should see

      Rising, but more and more slowly. That always happens just before a relative maximum, between an inflection point and the top.

    4. In the second lab, set the interval to [−0.5, 4.5]. Where are the absolute max and min?

      What you should see

      Both at the endpoints: f(4.5) ≈ 11.1 beats the relative max 5, and f(−0.5) ≈ −5.1 is below the relative min 1.

    5. Shrink the interval to [0.5, 3.5]. Now what?

      What you should see

      Now the turning points win: absolute max 5 at x = 1 and absolute min 1 at x = 3. Always check both the turning points and the ends.

    Worked example: reading a cubic

    For f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 1 (graphed), give the intervals where f increases and decreases, the relative extrema, the point of inflection, and the absolute extrema on [−0.5, 4.5].

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Increasing and decreasing. From the graph, f increases on (−∞, 1) and (3, ∞) and decreases on (1, 3).
    2. Relative extrema. Increasing then decreasing at x = 1: relative max f(1) = 1 − 6 + 9 + 1 = 5. Decreasing then increasing at x = 3: relative min f(3) = 27 − 54 + 27 + 1 = 1.
    3. Inflection. Concave down to the left of x = 2 and up to the right: inflection at (2, 3), halfway between the turning points.
    4. Absolute extrema on [−0.5, 4.5]. Compare f(−0.5) = −5.125, f(1) = 5, f(3) = 1, f(4.5) = 11.125. Absolute max 11.125 at x = 4.5, absolute min −5.125 at x = −0.5: both at the endpoints.

    Worked example 2: the biggest box

    Cut a square of side x cm from each corner of a 20 cm × 30 cm card and fold up the sides to make an open box. Write the volume V(x), give its domain, and use a graphing calculator to find the largest volume.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Dimensions. Height x, width 20 − 2x, length 30 − 2x. So V(x) = x(20 − 2x)(30 − 2x), a cubic.
    2. Domain. Every side must be positive: x > 0 and 20 − 2x > 0, so 0 < x < 10.
    3. Maximum. On (0, 10) the graph rises, turns and falls. The calculator gives the relative max at x ≈ 3.92 cm, with V ≈ 3.92 × 12.15 × 22.15 ≈ 1056 cm³.
    4. Check. V(2) = 2 × 16 × 26 = 832 and V(6) = 6 × 8 × 18 = 864, both less. On the open interval (0, 10) the turning point is the absolute maximum.

    Common mistakes

    • Giving the x-value when asked for the maximum value (the output), or the other way around.
    • Forgetting the endpoints when finding an absolute extremum on a closed interval.
    • Calling every point where the graph looks flat a turning point: x³ flattens at 0 but keeps increasing.
    • Confusing a point of inflection (bend switches) with a turning point (direction switches).

    Why at most n − 1 turning points

    Each turning point is where the rate of change switches sign. For a polynomial of degree n, the rate of change behaves like a polynomial of degree n − 1 (you will see why in calculus), which has at most n − 1 zeros. So the direction can switch at most n − 1 times, and the bending at most n − 2 times.

    Check yourself: What is the greatest number of relative extrema a degree-6 polynomial can have?

    Check yourself: f increases on (−∞, 2) and decreases on (2, ∞). Which is true?

    AP Unit 1On the AP examCED 1.5

    Zeros & complex zeros

    Every zero of a polynomial is a factor. Count them with multiplicity, include the complex ones, and a degree-n polynomial has exactly n.

    The idea

    If f(a) = 0 then (x − a) is a factor of f, and a is a zero (an x-intercept when a is real). If the factor appears k times, a has multiplicity k. At a zero of odd multiplicity the graph crosses the x-axis (the sign changes); at even multiplicity it touches and turns back (no sign change). Higher multiplicity flattens the graph near the zero.

    A polynomial of degree n has exactly n complex zeros, counting multiplicity (the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra). Some can be non-real, like 1 + i. If the coefficients are real, non-real zeros come in conjugate pairs a + bi and a − bi, so a real cubic always has at least one real zero.

    Factors give you the sign of f between zeros, which solves polynomial inequalities. Symmetry is another shortcut: f is even if f(−x) = f(x) (mirror image in the y-axis, like x⁴ − x²) and odd if f(−x) = −f(x) (symmetric about the origin, like x³ − 4x).

    Cross, touch or flatten: 8 zeros

    The shape at a zero tells you how many times its factor repeats.

    1. What is the multiplicity of the zero marked in orange?

    A squared factor never changes sign, so the graph touches the axis and turns back, like a parabola. Here f(x) = (x + 2)(x − 1)².

    2. What is the multiplicity of the zero marked in orange?

    A simple zero: the factor changes sign there, so the graph crosses the axis like a line. Here f(x) = (x + 2)(x − 1)².

    3. What is the multiplicity of the zero marked in orange?

    A cubed factor changes sign but is very flat near its zero, so the graph levels off as it crosses, like y = x³. Here f(x) = x³.

    4. What is the multiplicity of the zero marked in orange?

    A cubed factor changes sign but is very flat near its zero, so the graph levels off as it crosses, like y = x³. Here f(x) = (x − 1.5)³(x + 1).

    5. What is the multiplicity of the zero marked in orange?

    A squared factor never changes sign, so the graph touches the axis and turns back, like a parabola. Here f(x) = −(x + 1)²(x − 2).

    6. What is the multiplicity of the zero marked in orange?

    A simple zero: the factor changes sign there, so the graph crosses the axis like a line. Here f(x) = (x + 2)x(x − 2).

    7. What is the multiplicity of the zero marked in orange?

    A squared factor never changes sign, so the graph touches the axis and turns back, like a parabola. Here f(x) = x²(x − 2)².

    8. What is the multiplicity of the zero marked in orange?

    A cubed factor changes sign but is very flat near its zero, so the graph levels off as it crosses, like y = x³. Here f(x) = (x + 1)³(x − 2)².

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Tap the middle zero until it has multiplicity 2. What does the graph do there?

      What you should see

      It touches the axis and turns back: (x − a)² is never negative, so f does not change sign there.

    2. Give one zero multiplicity 3. How is it different from multiplicity 1?

      What you should see

      It still crosses (odd multiplicity), but it flattens out as it crosses, like y = x³.

    3. Drag the zeros to −2, 0 and 2, all multiplicity 1. What symmetry appears?

      What you should see

      f(x) = (x + 2)x(x − 2) = x³ − 4x is odd: rotating the graph 180° about the origin gives the same graph.

    4. In the second lab, slide k from 1 down to −1. Watch the left picture. What happens at k = 0?

      What you should see

      The two non-real zeros 1 ± i slide toward the real axis, meet at k = 0 (a double zero at 1, where the graph touches), then split into two real zeros. There are always 3 zeros in total.

    5. With k = 2, how many x-intercepts does the graph have? How many zeros does f have?

      What you should see

      One x-intercept (x = −2), but three zeros: −2 and the conjugate pair p ± i√2. Non-real zeros do not show up on the graph.

    Worked example: from zeros to a formula

    A degree-4 polynomial f with real coefficients has a zero of multiplicity 2 at x = 2, and 1 + i is also a zero. If f(0) = 8, find f(x).

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Count the zeros. Degree 4 means 4 zeros with multiplicity: 2, 2, and 1 + i. The fourth must be the conjugate 1 − i.
    2. Pair the conjugates. (x − (1 + i))(x − (1 − i)) = (x − 1)² − i² = x² − 2x + 2, which has real coefficients.
    3. Write the form. f(x) = a(x − 2)²(x² − 2x + 2). Then f(0) = a(4)(2) = 8a = 8, so a = 1.
    4. Answer. f(x) = (x − 2)²(x² − 2x + 2) = x⁴ − 6x³ + 14x² − 16x + 8. Only one x-intercept, at 2, where the graph touches.

    Worked example 2: when is the business profitable?

    A company's monthly profit is P(q) = −q³ + 12q² − 20q thousand dollars when it sells q thousand units. For which q is the profit positive?

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Factor. P(q) = −q(q² − 12q + 20) = −q(q − 2)(q − 10). Zeros: 0, 2, 10, each multiplicity 1, so the sign changes at each.
    2. Test the sign. For 0 < q < 2, try q = 1: −1(−1)(−9) = −9 < 0. For 2 < q < 10, try q = 5: −5(3)(−5) = 75 > 0. For q > 10, try q = 11: −11(9)(1) = −99 < 0.
    3. Answer. P(q) > 0 for 2 < q < 10: between 2,000 and 10,000 units.
    4. Meaning. Below 2,000 units fixed costs eat the profit; above 10,000 the model says extra production costs more than it earns. The zeros are the break-even points.

    Common mistakes

    • Forgetting the conjugate: if 3 − 2i is a zero of a real polynomial, so is 3 + 2i.
    • Counting x-intercepts as the number of zeros: non-real zeros have no x-intercept.
    • Saying a graph crosses at a squared factor.
    • Writing the factor for the zero −4 as (x − 4) instead of (x + 4).

    Why conjugates come in pairs

    If f has real coefficients and f(a + bi) = 0, take the complex conjugate of the whole equation. Conjugating a sum or product conjugates each piece, and the real coefficients stay the same, so f(a − bi) = 0 too. Multiplying the pair gives x² − 2ax + (a² + b²), a quadratic with real coefficients and no real zeros.

    Check yourself: A polynomial with real coefficients has zeros 4 and 2 − 3i. Which must also be a zero?

    End behavior

    Far from the origin, a polynomial looks like its leading term. Degree and sign alone decide where the ends go.

    The idea

    For very large |x|, the highest-power term of a polynomial is so much bigger than the others that it decides everything: the end behavior of f(x) = aₙxⁿ + … + a₀ is the same as that of its leading term aₙxⁿ. The middle can wiggle; the ends cannot.

    Two facts settle the ends. Even degree: both ends go the same way, up if aₙ > 0 and down if aₙ < 0. Odd degree: the ends go opposite ways, down on the left and up on the right if aₙ > 0, the reverse if aₙ < 0.

    Write it with limits: limx→∞ f(x) = ∞ means f(x) grows without bound as x does. For example, for f(x) = −2x³ + 5x, limx→∞ f(x) = −∞ and limx→−∞ f(x) = ∞. For a factored polynomial, multiply the leading terms of the factors to get the leading term.

    even n, aₙ < 0down and down

    Zoom out: 8 end behaviors

    Predict the ends from the formula, then zoom out. The wiggles in the middle do not matter.

    1. Zoom out on y = x³ − 4x. What do the ends do?

    The leading term is x³: degree 3 (odd), coefficient positive. Odd degree: the ends go opposite ways.

    2. Zoom out on y = −x⁴ + 3x² + 1. What do the ends do?

    The leading term is −x⁴: degree 4 (even), coefficient negative. Even degree: both ends go the same way.

    3. Zoom out on y = −x³ + 2x². What do the ends do?

    The leading term is −x³: degree 3 (odd), coefficient negative. Odd degree: the ends go opposite ways.

    4. Zoom out on y = x⁴ − 5x² + 4. What do the ends do?

    The leading term is x⁴: degree 4 (even), coefficient positive. Even degree: both ends go the same way.

    5. Zoom out on y = −0.5x⁵ + 4x³ − 2. What do the ends do?

    The leading term is −0.5x⁵: degree 5 (odd), coefficient negative. Odd degree: the ends go opposite ways.

    6. Zoom out on y = (x − 1)²(x + 1)(x − 3). What do the ends do?

    The leading term is x⁴: degree 4 (even), coefficient positive. Even degree: both ends go the same way.

    7. Zoom out on y = −(x + 2)(x − 1)². What do the ends do?

    The leading term is −x³: degree 3 (odd), coefficient negative. Odd degree: the ends go opposite ways.

    8. Zoom out on y = 3 − x². What do the ends do?

    The leading term is −x²: degree 2 (even), coefficient negative. Even degree: both ends go the same way.

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose x³ − 6x² + 4 and zoom out slowly. When do the two graphs look alike?

      What you should see

      Near the origin they look nothing alike. By a half-width of about 100, the ratio f(x)/x³ at the edge is above 0.9 and the curves are almost on top of each other.

    2. Choose −(x − 3)²(x + 1). What is its leading term without expanding?

      What you should see

      Multiply the leading terms of the factors: −(x²)(x) = −x³. Odd degree, negative: up on the left, down on the right.

    3. In the second lab, keep a > 0 and step n from 1 to 6. What alternates?

      What you should see

      Odd n: down on the left, up on the right. Even n: up on both ends. Only the parity of n and the sign of a matter.

    4. Switch to a < 0. What happens to every picture?

      What you should see

      It flips upside down (a reflection in the x-axis), so every arrow flips.

    5. Set n = 2 and then n = 8. How are the shapes different, and is the end behavior?

      What you should see

      x⁸ is flatter near 0 and steeper outside [−1, 1], but both go up on both ends: same end behavior.

    Worked example: end behavior from the formula

    Describe the end behavior of f(x) = −2x⁵ + 30x³ + x − 7 with limits, and show that the leading term dominates.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Leading term. −2x⁵: degree 5 (odd), coefficient −2 (negative).
    2. Ends. Odd and negative: limx→∞ f(x) = −∞ and limx→−∞ f(x) = ∞.
    3. Check at x = 10. f(10) = −200,000 + 30,000 + 10 − 7 = −169,997, and −2(10⁵) = −200,000: ratio ≈ 0.85.
    4. At x = 100. The ratio is ≈ 0.9985. The other terms matter less and less: f(x)/(−2x⁵) → 1.

    Worked example 2: a model that runs out

    A town's population t years after 1990 was modeled by P(t) = −0.1t³ + 3t² + 40t + 500 for 0 ≤ t ≤ 30. What does the model predict in the long run, and when does it predict the town is empty?

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. On the data. P(0) = 500, P(10) = 1100, P(20) = 1700, P(30) = 1700: the model fits growth that is leveling off.
    2. End behavior. Leading term −0.1t³: limt→∞ P(t) = −∞. The model must eventually predict a falling, then negative, population.
    3. When P = 0. A graphing calculator gives t ≈ 42.3, around 2032, after a peak of about 1813 near t ≈ 25.
    4. Lesson. A cubic fit is reasonable near its data, but its end behavior is set by its leading term, not by the town. Do not extrapolate far.

    Common mistakes

    • Using the constant term or the first term written instead of the highest-power term.
    • Forgetting the sign of the leading coefficient.
    • Thinking the middle wiggles change the end behavior.
    • For a factored form, adding degrees wrongly: (x − 1)²(x + 2)³ has degree 5.

    Why the leading term wins

    Factor out the leading term: f(x) = aₙxⁿ(1 + (aₙ₋₁/aₙ)/x + … + (a₀/aₙ)/xⁿ). Every term in the parentheses except the 1 has x in a denominator, so it shrinks toward 0 as |x| grows. The parentheses approach 1, and f(x) behaves like aₙxⁿ.

    Check yourself: Which describes f(x) = 4 − 3x⁶ + x⁵?

    Rational functions

    A ratio of polynomials can blow up where the denominator is zero and settle down far away. Its zeros and asymptotes give the whole skeleton of the graph.

    The idea

    A rational function is a ratio of two polynomials, f(x) = p(x)/q(x). It is not defined where q(x) = 0. The zeros of f are the zeros of p, as long as q is not also 0 there. At each zero of q that is not cancelled, the graph has a vertical asymptote: the outputs grow without bound, positive or negative, as x approaches it.

    Far away, only the leading terms matter, as with polynomials. If deg p < deg q the outputs shrink toward 0: horizontal asymptote y = 0. If deg p = deg q they approach the ratio of leading coefficients: y = aₙ/bₙ. If deg p > deg q there is no horizontal asymptote: f keeps growing (when the degrees differ by exactly 1 it follows a slanted line, found by division).

    At a vertical asymptote x = c, look at the sign of f on each side: it depends on the sign of the factors and on whether the factor (x − c) appears an odd or even number of times. An odd power: the two sides go opposite ways (one to +∞, one to −∞). An even power: both sides go the same way. Write it as limx→c⁺ f(x) = ∞.

    Far away: 8 rational functions

    Compare the degrees of the top and the bottom, predict the far-away behavior, then see it.

    1. What happens to f(x) = 2x / (x² + 1) far to the left and right?

    The numerator has the smaller degree, so the bottom wins far away: the outputs shrink to 0.

    2. What happens to f(x) = (3x² − 1) / (x² + 2) far to the left and right?

    The degrees are equal, so the ratio of the leading coefficients is the horizontal asymptote.

    3. What happens to f(x) = (x² + 1) / (x − 1) far to the left and right?

    The numerator has the bigger degree, so the outputs keep growing: no horizontal asymptote. Dividing gives the slanted line it follows.

    4. What happens to f(x) = (−2x + 5) / (x − 4) far to the left and right?

    The degrees are equal, so the ratio of the leading coefficients is the horizontal asymptote.

    5. What happens to f(x) = 4 / (x² + 1) far to the left and right?

    The numerator has the smaller degree, so the bottom wins far away: the outputs shrink to 0.

    6. What happens to f(x) = x³ / (x² − 4) far to the left and right?

    The numerator has the bigger degree, so the outputs keep growing: no horizontal asymptote. Dividing gives the slanted line it follows.

    7. What happens to f(x) = (5x² + x) / (2x² − 3) far to the left and right?

    The degrees are equal, so the ratio of the leading coefficients is the horizontal asymptote.

    8. What happens to f(x) = (x + 1) / (x² + x + 2) far to the left and right?

    The numerator has the smaller degree, so the bottom wins far away: the outputs shrink to 0.

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose Equal. Where does the graph level off, and does it ever cross that line?

      What you should see

      It levels off at y = the ratio of leading coefficients (2 when the ratio is 2). It can cross its horizontal asymptote in the middle; the asymptote describes only the far ends.

    2. Choose Top smaller. What is the horizontal asymptote? What happens at the zeros?

      What you should see

      y = 0, the x-axis, because the bottom grows faster. The graph crosses the axis at each zero.

    3. Choose Top one bigger. Is there a horizontal asymptote?

      What you should see

      No: the outputs keep growing. The graph follows a slanted line far out, which you can find by dividing.

    4. Move Zero 1 until it sits on top of Pole 1. What happens to the asymptote?

      What you should see

      It disappears and becomes a hole: the factor cancels. That is the next module.

    5. In the second lab, set power 1 and then power 2. What changes on the left side?

      What you should see

      With power 1 the sides go opposite ways. With power 2 the factor (x − 2)² is never negative, so both sides go the same direction.

    Worked example: reading a rational function

    For f(x) = (x − 1)(x + 2) / ((x − 3)(x + 1)), find the zeros, the vertical asymptotes, the horizontal asymptote, and the sign of f just to the right of x = 3.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Zeros. The numerator is 0 at x = 1 and x = −2, and the denominator is not 0 there: zeros 1 and −2.
    2. Vertical asymptotes. The denominator is 0 at x = 3 and x = −1, and nothing cancels: x = 3 and x = −1.
    3. Horizontal asymptote. Degrees are equal (2 and 2); leading coefficients 1 and 1: y = 1.
    4. Right of x = 3. At x = 4: (3)(6)/((1)(5)) = 3.6 > 0, so f(x) → +∞ as x → 3⁺. At x = 2: (1)(4)/((−1)(3)) = −4/3, so f → −∞ from the left: opposite sides, as expected for an odd power.

    Worked example 2: cost per unit

    Making n units costs a $500 setup fee plus $8 per unit, so the average cost per unit is A(n) = (500 + 8n)/n. Find A(10), A(50) and A(100), and describe what happens as n gets large.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. A(10) = (500 + 80)/10 = $58.
    2. A(50) = (500 + 400)/50 = $18. A(100) = (500 + 800)/100 = $13.
    3. Large n. Equal degrees (1 and 1), leading coefficients 8 and 1: horizontal asymptote y = 8. A(n) = 8 + 500/n, so the setup fee gets spread over more and more units.
    4. Meaning. The average cost keeps falling toward the $8 per-unit cost but never reaches it. At n → 0⁺ it blows up: a vertical asymptote at n = 0.

    Common mistakes

    • Thinking a graph can never cross its horizontal asymptote. It can, in the middle.
    • Cancelling terms instead of factors, like (x + 2)/(x + 3) → 2/3.
    • Writing a vertical asymptote as a y-value. A vertical asymptote is x = c.
    • Forgetting that a zero of the denominator that also cancels is a hole, not an asymptote.

    Why equal degrees give the ratio of leading coefficients

    Divide the top and the bottom by the highest power of x. Every other term then has x in its denominator and shrinks toward 0, leaving the ratio of the leading coefficients. For (3x² − 5)/(2x² + 7x): divide by x² to get (3 − 5/x²)/(2 + 7/x) → 3/2.

    Holes

    When a factor appears in both the numerator and the denominator, the graph has a single missing point instead of an asymptote.

    The idea

    Factor the top and the bottom of a rational function. A factor (x − c) in both means f is undefined at x = c, but it cancels everywhere else. After cancelling, the graph looks exactly like the simpler function, except for one missing point: a hole at x = c, drawn as an open circle.

    To find the hole, cancel the common factor, then plug x = c into what is left. That output is the height of the open circle. The original function is undefined there, but the outputs get closer and closer to this number from both sides: limx→c f(x) exists and equals it.

    Careful with multiplicity: if (x − c) appears more times in the denominator than in the numerator, some of it is left in the denominator after cancelling and x = c is still a vertical asymptote. A hole happens only when the factor is cancelled completely from the bottom.

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose top 1, bottom 1. Where is the open circle, and is there an asymptote at x = h?

      What you should see

      The open circle sits at x = h with the height of the simplified function. There is no asymptote at h: the factor cancelled completely.

    2. Choose top 1, bottom 2. What happens now at x = h?

      Cancelling one factor leaves (x − h) in the denominator, so there is a vertical asymptote at h. No hole.

    3. Choose top 2, bottom 1. Why is there a hole and also a zero at h?

      What you should see

      One factor cancels (hole at x = h) and one is left in the numerator, so the simplified function has a zero there: the hole sits on the x-axis.

    4. In the second lab, choose (x² − 4)/(x − 2) and slide the zoom down to 0.02. What do you see?

      What you should see

      The graph is a straight line with a tiny gap at x = 2 that never closes, however far you zoom. The outputs near 2 are all close to 4.

    5. Choose 1/(x − 2) and zoom in the same way. What is different?

      What you should see

      The outputs get larger and larger: no number to settle on. That is an asymptote, not a hole.

    Worked example: finding a hole

    Find the hole and any vertical asymptote of f(x) = (x² − x − 6)/(x − 3). Sketch the graph.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Factor. x² − x − 6 = (x − 3)(x + 2), so f(x) = (x − 3)(x + 2)/(x − 3).
    2. Cancel. For x ≠ 3, f(x) = x + 2: a line. The factor (x − 3) is gone from the denominator, so no vertical asymptote.
    3. The hole. f(3) is undefined, but the line has height 3 + 2 = 5 there: hole at (3, 5).
    4. Sketch. Draw y = x + 2 and put an open circle at (3, 5). The outputs get closer and closer to 5 on both sides: lim f(x) = 5 as x → 3.

    Worked example 2: a spreadsheet error

    A shop's margin per unit at price x dollars is M(x) = (x² − 100)/(x − 10). The spreadsheet shows #DIV/0! at x = 10. What should the margin be there?

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Factor. x² − 100 = (x − 10)(x + 10), so M(x) = (x − 10)(x + 10)/(x − 10).
    2. Cancel. For x ≠ 10, M(x) = x + 10.
    3. At x = 10. The graph is a line with a hole at (10, 20). The spreadsheet cannot divide by 0, but the values approach $20.
    4. Check. M(9.9) = 19.9, M(10.1) = 20.1: the margin passes smoothly through 20 on both sides.

    Common mistakes

    • Cancelling terms instead of factors.
    • Saying a hole is an asymptote, or the other way around: look at what is left in the denominator.
    • Finding the hole height from the original formula (it is undefined there). Use the simplified one.
    • Forgetting to factor completely before deciding.

    A hole is a removable discontinuity

    If you simply define f(c) to be the missing height, the gap closes and the graph becomes one unbroken line. That is why holes are called removable. A vertical asymptote cannot be repaired by choosing one number.

    Equivalent forms

    Factored, expanded, divided: the same function can be written many ways, and each way shows something different.

    The idea

    A polynomial can be written factored, a(x − r₁)(x − r₂)…, or expanded, aₙxⁿ + … + a₀. Factored form shows the zeros and their multiplicities. Expanded form shows the degree, the leading term and the y-intercept a₀. Converting between them means multiplying out or factoring.

    To divide polynomials, use long division or, when dividing by (x − r), synthetic division. The result: p(x) = d(x)·q(x) + R(x), where the remainder R has smaller degree than the divisor d. For a divisor (x − r) the remainder is a number, and it equals p(r): the Remainder Theorem. If the remainder is 0, then (x − r) is a factor.

    Dividing the whole equation by d(x) gives a rational function as a quotient plus a remainder term: p(x)/d(x) = q(x) + R(x)/d(x). Far from the origin, R/d shrinks to 0, so the rational function follows q(x): for a quotient of degree 1 this is the slanted line (oblique asymptote).

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Set the coefficients to 1, 0, −7, 6 with r = 2. What is the remainder, and what does it tell you?

      What you should see

      The remainder is 0: p(2) = 8 − 14 + 6 = 0, so (x − 2) is a factor. The quotient x² + 2x − 3 factors further as (x + 3)(x − 1).

    2. Change the constant to 7. What is the remainder now, and how does it compare with p(2)?

      What you should see

      The remainder is 1, and p(2) = 1: the Remainder Theorem. The remainder is just the output at r.

    3. Press Next step repeatedly. Which numbers get multiplied by r?

      What you should see

      Each result from the bottom row gets multiplied by r and written under the next coefficient, then added. Bring down, multiply, add, repeat.

    4. In the second lab, set x = 8. How much of f(x) comes from the remainder term?

      What you should see

      Almost none: R/d = 9/7 ≈ 1.29, compared with a quotient value of 12. The farther out you go, the smaller the remainder term and the closer f is to the slanted line.

    5. Move x close to the vertical asymptote. Which part dominates?

      What you should see

      The remainder term R/d: it grows without bound as d → 0, while the quotient stays moderate. Near an asymptote the remainder wins; far away the quotient wins.

    Worked example: dividing a volume

    A box has volume V(x) = 2x³ + 9x² + 7x − 6 and one dimension (x + 3). Find the other two dimensions.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Set up. Divide V(x) by (x + 3) = (x − (−3)), so r = −3, with coefficients 2, 9, 7, −6.
    2. Synthetic division. Bring down 2. 2 × (−3) = −6; 9 − 6 = 3. 3 × (−3) = −9; 7 − 9 = −2. (−2) × (−3) = 6; −6 + 6 = 0.
    3. Read it. The quotient is 2x² + 3x − 2 with remainder 0, which confirms that (x + 3) is a factor.
    4. Factor the quotient. 2x² + 3x − 2 = (2x − 1)(x + 2). The dimensions are (x + 3), (2x − 1) and (x + 2).

    Worked example 2: cost per ticket

    The total cost of making n tickets is n² + 12n + 500 dollars, so the average cost per ticket is A(n) = (n² + 12n + 500)/(n + 4). Rewrite A(n) as a quotient plus remainder and say what happens for large n.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Divide. (n + 4)(n + 8) = n² + 12n + 32, and 500 − 32 = 468: n² + 12n + 500 = (n + 4)(n + 8) + 468.
    2. Rewrite. A(n) = n + 8 + 468/(n + 4).
    3. Large n. The fraction 468/(n + 4) shrinks toward 0, so A(n) follows the slanted line y = n + 8: no horizontal asymptote, a slanted one.
    4. Check. A(20) = 28 + 468/24 = 28 + 19.5 = 47.5. Directly: (400 + 240 + 500)/24 = 1140/24 = 47.5 ✓.

    Common mistakes

    • Forgetting a 0 for a missing term: dividing x³ − 7x + 6 means the coefficients are 1, 0, −7, 6.
    • Using r with the wrong sign: dividing by (x + 3) uses r = −3.
    • Calling the last number the last coefficient of the quotient: it is the remainder.
    • Cancelling terms across a sum in a fraction.

    Why the remainder is p(r)

    Write p(x) = (x − r)q(x) + R. Put x = r: p(r) = 0·q(r) + R = R. So the remainder is exactly the value of p at r. That makes division a fast way to test whether r is a zero: if the remainder is 0, you have a zero and a factor at the same time.

    Check yourself: p(x) = x³ − 2x² − 5x + 6. What is the remainder when p is divided by (x − 3)?

    Check yourself: (x² + 5x + 7)/(x + 2) = x + 3 + R/(x + 2). What is R?

    AP Unit 1On the AP examCED 1.12

    Transformations of functions

    Shift, stretch and flip any graph with four numbers, and track what happens to every point.

    The idea

    Start from a graph y = f(x) and build a new one: g(x) = a·f(b(x − h)) + k. Each number does one job. h shifts right by h (left if negative). k shifts up by k. a stretches vertically by |a| and flips the graph over the x-axis when a is negative. b compresses horizontally by a factor of 1/|b| and flips over the y-axis when b is negative.

    Follow a point. If (x, y) is on the graph of f, then (x/b + h, a·y + k) is on the graph of g. The horizontal changes act on x and look backwards (b makes the graph narrower, h = 2 moves it right); the vertical changes act on y and look natural. To apply them in order: horizontal stretch or flip by b, then shift by h, then vertical stretch or flip by a, then shift by k.

    Transformations pass properties on. Zeros of g are at x/b + h for each zero x of f. The range of g is a·(range of f) + k, reversed if a is negative. Even and odd symmetry, intercepts and asymptotes all move with the graph. And any two graphs of the same shape at different sizes and places are related this way: the tide at one harbor and the tide at another.

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose the four-point graph. Set a = −1. What does each key point do?

      What you should see

      The graph flips over the x-axis: each point (x, y) goes to (x, −y).

    2. Set b = 2 (a = 1). Does the graph get wider or narrower?

      What you should see

      Narrower: every x-coordinate is halved. A bigger b squeezes the graph, a trap for beginners.

    3. Set h = 2. Is that left or right? Which numbers change?

      What you should see

      Right: g(x) = f(x − 2) needs x one bigger to do what f did, so each point moves 2 to the right. Only the x-coordinates change.

    4. Choose 1/x and set k = 2. What happens to the horizontal asymptote?

      What you should see

      It moves up with the graph, from y = 0 to y = 2. Asymptotes are transformed like everything else.

    5. In the second lab choose the first example and drag the stage slider from 0 to 4. At which stage does the graph flip over?

      What you should see

      At stage 3, the vertical stretch by a = −2: it stretches by 2 and flips. The shift by k = 1 in stage 4 then lifts it, but does not change its shape.

    Worked example: moving key points

    The graph of f passes through (−2, 1), (0, 3), (2, −1) and (4, 0). Find the images of these points on the graph of g(x) = −2f(2(x − 1)) + 1.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Read the numbers. a = −2, b = 2, h = 1, k = 1.
    2. Horizontal. x → x/b + h = x/2 + 1. The x-values −2, 0, 2, 4 become 0, 1, 2, 3.
    3. Vertical. y → a·y + k = −2y + 1. The y-values 1, 3, −1, 0 become −1, −5, 3, 1.
    4. Answer. The graph of g passes through (0, −1), (1, −5), (2, 3) and (3, 1). It is flipped and stretched vertically, squeezed horizontally and moved right 1 and up 1.

    Worked example 2: tides at two harbors

    At harbor A, the tide height is h_A(t) meters, with a high tide of 7 m at t = 0 and a low of 1 m at t = 6 hours. At harbor B the same tide arrives 2 hours later and is 1.5 times as high. Write h_B in terms of h_A, and find its high and low.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Later. A delay of 2 hours is a shift right by 2: replace t by t − 2.
    2. Higher. 1.5 times as high is a vertical stretch by 1.5: multiply the whole thing.
    3. Formula. h_B(t) = 1.5·h_A(t − 2).
    4. Key points. High tide: (0, 7) → (2, 1.5 · 7) = (2, 10.5). Low tide: (6, 1) → (8, 1.5 · 1) = (8, 1.5). The range goes from [1, 7] to [1.5, 10.5].

    Common mistakes

    • Moving the wrong way for h: g(x) = f(x − 2) moves RIGHT.
    • Thinking b = 2 widens the graph. It narrows it by a factor of 2.
    • Doing the shifts before the stretches: f(2x − 2) is a shift by 1 after the squeeze, not by 2.
    • Forgetting that a vertical shift k also moves asymptotes and the range.

    Why the horizontal changes look backwards

    For g(x) = f(2x), the output at x is what f produced at 2x, so g reaches f's value at x = 1 where f reached it at x = 2. The graph gets there twice as fast, so it is squeezed. In the same way g(x) = f(x − 2) at x = 5 gives f(3): g repeats f's outputs two units later, to the right.

    Check yourself: The graph of f has a zero at x = 4. Where is a zero of g(x) = f(2(x + 1))?

    Check yourself: f has range [−3, 5]. What is the range of g(x) = −2f(x) + 1?

    AP Unit 1On the AP examCED 1.13CED 1.14

    Building function models

    Choose the kind of function that fits the situation, say what you are assuming, and use the model with care.

    The idea

    A function model is a function that describes a real situation. To select one, look at the data and the context. Constant first differences: linear. Constant second differences: quadratic. Outputs that level off toward a value (like cost per unit): rational. A graph that changes behavior at a known point: piecewise. A shape that rises, falls and rises again: cubic or higher.

    Every model carries assumptions: that growth stays the same, that the shape continues, that no other factors matter. State them, check them against the data, and say where the model should not be trusted, especially outside the range of the data (extrapolation). A residual is data minus model: random residuals say the model fits; a pattern in the residuals says it does not.

    To construct a model: choose a type, find its parameters (from points, differences, a regression, or the context), state the domain, and use it to answer the question asked, with units. A piecewise function uses different formulas on different intervals, such as a bill with tiered rates; check what happens at the breakpoints.

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose Stopping distance with a linear model. What pattern do the residuals show?

      What you should see

      A U-shape: positive at both ends, negative in the middle. A pattern in the residuals means a line is the wrong kind of function.

    2. Switch to quadratic. What happens to the residuals?

      What you should see

      They shrink to almost nothing and show no pattern: the quadratic fits.

    3. Choose Cost per unit. Which model type fits best?

      What you should see

      The a/x + b model, with b near the per-unit cost. Quadratic and cubic fits can match the points but go wrong outside the data.

    4. In the second lab, set both rates to 0.12. What happens at the breakpoint?

      What you should see

      The kink disappears: it is a single line. A piecewise model needs different rates to be a genuinely different model.

    5. Move the breakpoint to 300. Does the bill at 800 kWh go up or down?

      What you should see

      Up: more of the usage is charged at the higher rate, so the 800 kWh bill rises.

    Worked example: choosing a model from a table

    A driver tests the stopping distance d (in feet) at several speeds v (in mph). Choose a model, find its formula, and predict d at 70 mph. Say what you are assuming.

    Stopping distance
    v (mph)2030405060
    d (ft)4482.5132192.5264

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. First differences (step 10): 38.5, 49.5, 60.5, 71.5. Not constant, so not linear.
    2. Second differences: 11, 11, 11. Constant: choose a quadratic. With step 10, 2a(10)² = 11, so a = 0.055.
    3. The rest. d = 0.055v² + bv + c. Using d(20) = 44 and d(30) = 82.5: 22 + 20b + c = 44 and 49.5 + 30b + c = 82.5, so b = 1.1 and c = 0. d = 0.055v² + 1.1v.
    4. Predict. d(70) = 0.055(4900) + 1.1(70) = 269.5 + 77 = 346.5 ft. This assumes the same road, tires and driver as in the test, and speeds beyond the data (extrapolation).

    Worked example 2: a tiered electricity bill

    An electric company charges a $10 fee plus $0.12 per kWh for the first 500 kWh, and $0.18 per kWh for each kWh above 500. Write the bill C(x) as a piecewise function and find the bill for 800 kWh.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. First piece (0 ≤ x ≤ 500): C(x) = 10 + 0.12x. At 500 kWh: 10 + 60 = $70.
    2. Second piece (x > 500): start from $70 and add $0.18 for each kWh above 500: C(x) = 70 + 0.18(x − 500).
    3. Piecewise form. C(x) = 10 + 0.12x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 500; C(x) = 70 + 0.18(x − 500) for x > 500.
    4. 800 kWh. C(800) = 70 + 0.18(300) = 70 + 54 = $124. The pieces meet at (500, 70), so the bill has no jump.

    Common mistakes

    • Choosing a model by its R² or how close it looks inside the data, without thinking about the context or what happens outside.
    • Extrapolating far beyond the data and trusting it.
    • Writing a piecewise function with pieces that do not meet when the story says they do.
    • Forgetting units, or the domain on which the model makes sense.

    No model is right; some are useful

    A model is a simplified description. A quadratic for stopping distance is right for the physics (braking distance grows with the square of speed), plus a term for reaction time. A cubic could fit the same five points but has no physical reason to. Good modeling joins the data to the story.

    AP Unit 2On the AP examCED 2.1

    Arithmetic & geometric sequences

    A sequence adds the same amount each step, or multiplies by the same factor each step. These two patterns are the seeds of linear and exponential functions.

    The idea

    A sequence is a list of numbers a₀, a₁, a₂, … : a function whose inputs are whole numbers. In an arithmetic sequence each term is the last plus a constant common difference d: aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + d. In a geometric sequence each term is the last times a constant common ratio r: aₙ = r·aₙ₋₁.

    Adding d, n times, gives an explicit formula: aₙ = a₀ + dn, a linear function of n. Multiplying by r, n times, gives aₙ = a₀·rⁿ, an exponential function of n. More generally, from any known term aₖ: aₙ = aₖ + d(n − k) or aₙ = aₖ·rⁿ⁻ᵏ.

    To tell them apart from data, look at differences and ratios of consecutive terms. Constant differences mean arithmetic; constant ratios mean geometric. If neither is constant, it is neither (a quadratic, for example, has constant second differences).

    Arithmetic, geometric or neither?

    Check the differences, then the ratios.

    1. Look at the terms. What kind of sequence is this?

    Arithmetic: each term is 4 more than the last.

    2. Look at the terms. What kind of sequence is this?

    Geometric: each term is 3 times the last.

    3. Look at the terms. What kind of sequence is this?

    Neither: the differences 3, 5, 7, 9 are not constant and the ratios 4, 2.25, … are not constant.

    4. Look at the terms. What kind of sequence is this?

    5. Look at the terms. What kind of sequence is this?

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose add d each step with a₀ = 2 and d = 3. What do the bars show?

      What you should see

      All the bars are the same height, 3. The dots rise along a straight line: constant change means linear.

    2. Switch to multiply with r = 1.5. Do the bars still stay the same?

      What you should see

      The differences grow, but the ratios stay at 1.5. For a geometric sequence it is the ratio that is constant, not the difference.

    3. Set r = 0.5. What happens to the terms?

      What you should see

      They shrink toward 0: multiplying by a number between 0 and 1 is decay. The differences are negative and shrinking in size.

    4. In the second lab choose aₙ = 2·aₙ₋₁ and set n = 10. Which is quicker: building up, or jumping?

      What you should see

      Jumping: a₁₀ = 1·2¹⁰ = 1024 takes one calculation, while the chain takes ten. That is why explicit formulas matter.

    Worked example: seats in a theater

    The first row of a theater has 20 seats and each row has 3 more seats than the row in front of it. Write a formula for the number of seats in row n, and find the first row with more than 100 seats.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Type. The same amount is added each row, so the sequence is arithmetic with first term 20 (row 1) and d = 3.
    2. Formula. From row 1: a(n) = 20 + 3(n − 1) = 3n + 17. Check: a(2) = 23 ✓.
    3. Solve. 3n + 17 > 100 gives 3n > 83, so n > 27.67.
    4. Answer. The first whole row number is 28. Check: a(27) = 98 and a(28) = 101.

    Worked example 2: a video catches on

    A video has 500 views on day 0, and each day it gets 1.2 times as many total views as the day before. Find the views on day 10 and the first day with more than 2000 views.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Type. Each day is multiplied by 1.2, so the sequence is geometric with a₀ = 500 and r = 1.2: vₙ = 500(1.2)ⁿ.
    2. Day 10. v₁₀ = 500(1.2)¹⁰ = 500(6.1917…) ≈ 3096 views.
    3. Day with more than 2000. Try values: v₇ = 500(3.5832) ≈ 1792 and v₈ = 500(4.2998) ≈ 2150.
    4. Answer. The first day above 2000 is day 8. (Later, logarithms will solve 500(1.2)ⁿ = 2000 directly: n ≈ 7.6.)

    Common mistakes

    • Calling a sequence arithmetic because the terms increase. Check that the differences are equal.
    • Using aₙ = a₀ + d·n with n starting at 1 when the first given term is a₁: use the term you know.
    • Dividing in the wrong order for the ratio: r = aₙ / aₙ₋₁, the later over the earlier.
    • Confusing the common difference with the common ratio.

    Sequences are functions

    A sequence is a function whose inputs are integers. Arithmetic sequences are the integer points of a line, and geometric sequences are the integer points of an exponential curve a·bˣ. The next modules turn these dots into continuous graphs, and the same two ideas, constant change versus constant factor, drive everything in Unit 2.

    Exponential functions

    Linear functions add the same amount each step; exponential functions multiply by the same factor. That one difference changes the whole shape of the graph.

    The idea

    Over equal-length input intervals, a linear function changes by a constant amount and an exponential function changes by a constant factor. A function of the form f(x) = a·bˣ (a ≠ 0, b > 0, b ≠ 1) is exponential: a is the initial value f(0), the y-intercept, and b is the growth factor, the number you multiply by for each step of 1 in x.

    If b > 1 the function is growth: with a > 0 it increases and is concave up; b = 1 + r where r is the percent increase per step. If 0 < b < 1 it is decay: with a > 0 it decreases, still concave up, and r = b − 1 is negative. A 15% growth rate means b = 1.15; a 12% loss means b = 0.88.

    The graph has a horizontal asymptote at y = 0. For a > 0, b > 1: as x → ∞ the outputs grow without bound, and as x → −∞ they approach 0. For 0 < b < 1 the two ends swap. The domain is all real numbers; the range is y > 0 (or y < 0 if a < 0). Exponential growth eventually beats any polynomial.

    Read the formula from the graph

    The y-intercept is a. One step right multiplies by b.

    1. Which function has this graph? (The two orange points are on it.)

    The y-intercept is a = 3 and each step right multiplies by b = f(1)/f(0) = 6/3 = 2. So the function is 3(2)ˣ. The factor is above 1, so it grows.

    2. Which function has this graph? (The two orange points are on it.)

    The y-intercept is a = 3 and each step right multiplies by b = f(1)/f(0) = 1.5/3 = 0.5. So the function is 3(0.5)ˣ. The factor is below 1, so it decays.

    3. Which function has this graph? (The two orange points are on it.)

    The y-intercept is a = 2 and each step right multiplies by b = f(1)/f(0) = 6/2 = 3. So the function is 2(3)ˣ. The factor is above 1, so it grows.

    4. Which function has this graph? (The two orange points are on it.)

    The y-intercept is a = 8 and each step right multiplies by b = f(1)/f(0) = 2/8 = 0.25. So the function is 8(0.25)ˣ. The factor is below 1, so it decays.

    5. Which function has this graph? (The two orange points are on it.)

    The y-intercept is a = 1 and each step right multiplies by b = f(1)/f(0) = 1.5/1 = 1.5. So the function is 1(1.5)ˣ. The factor is above 1, so it grows.

    6. Which function has this graph? (The two orange points are on it.)

    The y-intercept is a = 5 and each step right multiplies by b = f(1)/f(0) = 4/5 = 0.8. So the function is 5(0.8)ˣ. The factor is below 1, so it decays.

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Set a = 2 and b = 1.5. Where does the graph cross the y-axis, and what happens each time x goes up by 1?

      What you should see

      It crosses at y = 2 = a. Each step right multiplies the height by 1.5, shown by the dashed arrows.

    2. Slide b below 1. What kind of change is it?

      What you should see

      Decay: the graph falls toward the x-axis but never touches it. The x-axis is the horizontal asymptote, and the graph is still concave up.

    3. Set a = −2 with b = 1.5. What changes?

      What you should see

      The whole graph flips under the x-axis: the range is now y < 0. Still an asymptote at y = 0, but decreasing and concave down.

    4. In the second lab set b = 1.5 and step length 1. Compare the line and the curve at x = 6.

      What you should see

      The line adds 1 each step (it reaches 8) while the curve multiplies by 1.5 (it reaches about 22.8). Same start, same first step, very different futures.

    5. Make b = 1.1 and look at x = 6. Is the exponential far ahead of the line yet?

      What you should see

      Not by much: about 3.54 against 3.2. But the exponential is above the line for every x > 1 and the gap keeps widening, so give it time and it leaves the line far behind.

    Worked example: bacteria

    A colony starts with 800 bacteria and grows 15% each hour. Write a model for the number f(t) of bacteria after t hours, and estimate the number after 6 hours.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Growth factor. A 15% increase each hour multiplies the count by b = 1 + 0.15 = 1.15.
    2. Model. The initial value is 800, so f(t) = 800(1.15)ᵗ.
    3. Check one step. f(1) = 800(1.15) = 920, which is 15% more than 800 ✓.
    4. Evaluate. f(6) = 800(1.15)⁶ = 800(2.3131…) ≈ 1850 bacteria.

    Worked example 2: a car loses value

    A car costs $24,000 and loses 12% of its value each year. Model its value V(t) after t years and find the first whole year when it is worth less than $10,000.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Decay factor. Losing 12% leaves 88%, so b = 1 − 0.12 = 0.88.
    2. Model. V(t) = 24000(0.88)ᵗ.
    3. Try years. V(6) = 24000(0.4644) ≈ $11,146, still above 10,000. V(7) = 24000(0.4087) ≈ $9,808.
    4. Answer. The first whole year below $10,000 is year 7. (A logarithm will solve 24000(0.88)ᵗ = 10000 exactly: t ≈ 6.85.)

    Common mistakes

    • Writing b = 0.12 for a 12% decrease. The factor is 1 − 0.12 = 0.88.
    • Treating the exponential as if it adds a constant each step.
    • Thinking a decay graph crosses the x-axis. It approaches y = 0 but never reaches it.
    • Mixing up a (the starting value) with b (the factor).

    Exponential functions at a glance

    Equal steps in x give equal ratios in y: f(x + h)/f(x) = bʰ for every x. This is why constant percent change is exponential, and why a table with a constant ratio between outputs, when the inputs go up by equal steps, signals an exponential model.

    Periodic phenomena

    Tides, heartbeats, seasons and wheels all repeat. Learn one cycle and you know the whole function.

    The idea

    A function is periodic if its values repeat after a fixed horizontal distance p: f(x + p) = f(x) for every x. The smallest such positive p is the period. One period of the graph is a cycle; copy it end to end and you have the whole graph.

    Everything about one cycle repeats: where the function is increasing or decreasing, where it is concave up or down, its maximum and minimum, and its rates of change. So to find f(97) you only need to know where 97 lands inside one cycle: subtract whole periods.

    Two more words describe the vertical size: the midline is halfway between the maximum and minimum, (max + min)/2, and the amplitude is the distance from the midline to the maximum, (max − min)/2. Periodic functions do not have to be smooth waves: a heartbeat or a sawtooth is periodic too.

    Assumption upgrade

    Before
    functions either kept growing, kept shrinking, or turned around a few times
    So we didn't need
    a way to describe something that repeats forever
    Now
    many real quantities repeat on a schedule: time of day, season, rotation, a beat
    So we need
    period, cycle, midline and amplitude, and using the period to find values far away
    f(x + p) = f(x)p is the period
    midline = (max + min)/2
    amplitude = (max − min)/2
    f(x + kp) = f(x)any whole number k
    frequency = 1/periodcycles per unit
    Draw one cycle, get them all
    Start from
    f(x − p) = f(x) = f(x + p)—
    max · min—
    midline · amplitude—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. In the first lab, set x = 1 and slide p from 4 to 2. What stays matched?

      What you should see

      The three orange points always have the same height, one period apart: f(x − p) = f(x) = f(x + p). Changing p squeezes or stretches the cycle, and the copies follow.

    2. Choose Sawtooth, then drag a point in the gold band. Why does every tooth change?

      What you should see

      The whole graph is copies of the one cycle in the gold band. Change the cycle and every copy changes with it.

    3. Choose Pulse with p = 4. On which intervals is the function increasing, for all x?

      What you should see

      Find the increasing pieces inside one cycle, then add 4k. Whatever happens on [0, 4) happens again on [4, 8), [8, 12), and so on.

    4. In the second lab choose Heartbeat. Drag the cursors onto two neighboring tall spikes. What is the period and the heart rate?

      What you should see

      The spikes are 0.8 s apart, so the period is 0.8 s and the rate is 60 ÷ 0.8 = 75 beats per minute.

    5. Choose Mixed tide. Measure from one high tide to the next, then to the one after. Is the period 12.42 hours?

      What you should see

      No. Neighboring high tides have different heights, so the pattern only repeats after two of them: the period is about 24.84 hours. The period is the shortest shift that reproduces the whole graph, not just one feature.

    Worked example

    The graph shows a periodic function f. Find the period, midline and amplitude, then find f(13), f(10.5) and f(−2.5).

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Period. The pattern on [0, 4) repeats: period 4.
    2. Midline and amplitude. Max 3, min −1: midline (3 + (−1))/2 = 1, amplitude (3 − (−1))/2 = 2.
    3. f(13). 13 = 1 + 3(4), so f(13) = f(1) = 3.
    4. f(10.5). 10.5 = 2.5 + 2(4), so f(10.5) = f(2.5) = −1 (on the flat part).
    5. f(−2.5). Add a period: −2.5 + 4 = 1.5, so f(−2.5) = f(1.5). Halfway down from 3 (at x = 1) to −1 (at x = 2): 1.

    Worked example 2: reading a heart monitor

    A heart-monitor strip shows the tall spikes (R peaks) at t = 0.2 s and every 0.8 s after that. (a) What is the period? (b) What is the heart rate in beats per minute? (c) When is the 10th R peak?

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. The repeating feature. Measure from one R peak to the next; any repeated feature works, but the tall spike is easiest to read.
    2. (a) The peaks are 0.8 s apart, so the period is 0.8 s.
    3. (b) Frequency = 1/period = 1.25 beats per second, so 60 × 1.25 = 75 beats per minute, a normal resting rate.
    4. (c) The first peak is at 0.2 s and each later one adds 0.8 s, so the 10th is at 0.2 + 9(0.8) = 7.4 s.

    Common mistakes

    • Measuring the period between a maximum and the next minimum. That is half a period for a symmetric wave.
    • Thinking a periodic function must look like a sine wave.
    • Taking the period from two features that are not the same (a high tide and a slightly lower high tide).
    • Forgetting negative shifts: f(−2.5) = f(−2.5 + 4).
    • Calling (max − min) the amplitude. Amplitude is half of that.

    Why periods make predictions easy

    Once you know f on one cycle and the period p, every value is known. Write x = r + kp, where r is in the first cycle and k is a whole number; then f(x) = f(r). That is exactly how a calendar works: knowing what day of the week the 1st is tells you every date, because the week has period 7.

    Check yourself: A periodic function has period 6 and f(2) = 5. Which must be true?

    Check yourself: A Ferris wheel car is at the top every 40 seconds. What is the frequency?

    Sine, cosine & the unit circle

    An angle is a rotation. Turn a point around a circle of radius 1: its x-coordinate is the cosine and its y-coordinate is the sine.

    The idea

    Start at the point (1, 0) and rotate counterclockwise by an angle θ. Wherever you land on the unit circle (radius 1), the point is (cos θ, sin θ). That is the definition: no right triangle needed, so θ can be 125°, −30° or 7π.

    Angles are measured in radians: the length of arc the angle cuts on the unit circle. A full turn is 2π (about 6.28) radians, so 180° = π. On a circle of radius r the arc is r times longer: s = rθ.

    Every angle has a reference angle: the acute angle to the x-axis. The reference angle sets the sizes of sin and cos; the quadrant sets their signs. Learn quadrant I (0, π/6, π/4, π/3, π/2) and you know the whole circle.

    Assumption upgrade

    angles were between 0° and 90°, and sine and cosine were ratios of sides in a right triangle

    angles bigger than 90° or negative angles, or any picture of what sine does as the angle keeps growing
    Now
    sine and cosine are the coordinates of a point moving around a circle, so they repeat and can be negative
    So we need
    radians, the unit circle and the signs of sine, cosine and tangent in each quadrant
    point = (cos θ, sin θ)on the unit circle
    tan θ = sin θ / cos θslope of the radius
    radians = degrees × π/180180° = π
    sin²θ + cos²θ = 1the point is on the circle
    s = rθarc length, θ in radians

    Read the circle: 12 exact values

    Find the point first, then read the coordinate. The picture adds the triangle once you choose.

    1. sin(5π/6) = ?

    The angle lands quadrant II. Reference angle 30°, so the sizes are the quadrant I values; the signs come from the quadrant. The point is (−√3/2, 1/2), so sin(5π/6) = 1/2.

    2. cos(3π/4) = ?

    The angle lands quadrant II. Reference angle 45°, so the sizes are the quadrant I values; the signs come from the quadrant. The point is (−√2/2, √2/2), so cos(3π/4) = −√2/2.

    3. sin(4π/3) = ?

    The angle lands quadrant III. Reference angle 60°, so the sizes are the quadrant I values; the signs come from the quadrant. The point is (−1/2, −√3/2), so sin(4π/3) = −√3/2.

    4. cos(7π/4) = ?

    The angle lands quadrant IV. Reference angle 45°, so the sizes are the quadrant I values; the signs come from the quadrant. The point is (√2/2, −√2/2), so cos(7π/4) = √2/2.

    5. cos(2π/3) = ?

    The angle lands quadrant II. Reference angle 60°, so the sizes are the quadrant I values; the signs come from the quadrant. The point is (−1/2, √3/2), so cos(2π/3) = −1/2.

    6. sin(11π/6) = ?

    The angle lands quadrant IV. Reference angle 30°, so the sizes are the quadrant I values; the signs come from the quadrant. The point is (√3/2, −1/2), so sin(11π/6) = −1/2.

    7. cos(7π/6) = ?

    The angle lands quadrant III. Reference angle 30°, so the sizes are the quadrant I values; the signs come from the quadrant. The point is (−√3/2, −1/2), so cos(7π/6) = −√3/2.

    8. sin(5π/3) = ?

    The angle lands quadrant IV. Reference angle 60°, so the sizes are the quadrant I values; the signs come from the quadrant. The point is (1/2, −√3/2), so sin(5π/3) = −√3/2.

    9. cos(3π/2) = ?

    The angle lands on an axis. The point is (0, −1), so cos(3π/2) = 0.

    10. tan(5π/4) = ?

    The angle lands quadrant III. Reference angle 45°, so the sizes are the quadrant I values; the signs come from the quadrant. The point is (−√2/2, −√2/2), so tan(5π/4) = 1 (sin ÷ cos).

    11. sin(−π/6) = ?

    The angle lands quadrant IV. Reference angle 30°, so the sizes are the quadrant I values; the signs come from the quadrant. The point is (√3/2, −1/2), so sin(−π/6) = −1/2.

    12. sin(9π/4) = ?

    The angle lands quadrant I. Reference angle 45°, so the sizes are the quadrant I values; the signs come from the quadrant. The point is (√2/2, √2/2), so sin(9π/4) = √2/2.

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Set the angle to 125°. Which coordinate is negative, and why does the tangent come out negative?

      What you should see

      The point is in quadrant II: x = cos 125° ≈ −0.574 is negative and y = sin 125° ≈ 0.819 is positive. tan = sin/cos ≈ −1.428, negative because the signs differ: the radius slopes down to the right.

    2. Turn snapping on and step through 30°, 150°, 210° and 330°. What stays the same, and what changes?

      What you should see

      All four have reference angle 30°, so |sin| = 1/2 and |cos| = √3/2 every time. Only the signs change: (+,+) in I, (−,+) in II, (−,−) in III and (+,−) in IV.

    3. Slide to 90°. What happens to tan θ, and what does the orange tangent line do?

      What you should see

      cos 90° = 0, so tan 90° = 1/0 is undefined. The radius is vertical, and the line through it never meets the vertical line x = 1: the tangent segment runs off to infinity.

    4. Set 30°, then 390°, then −330°. Compare the points.

      What you should see

      All three are the same point (√3/2, 1/2). Angles that differ by a full turn (360° = 2π) are coterminal, which is why sine and cosine repeat with period 2π.

    5. In the second lab, keep θ = 1 and drag the radius from 1 to 3. What happens to the arc length and to y/r?

      What you should see

      The arc length s = rθ triples (from 1 to 3), but y/r stays sin 1 ≈ 0.841. The ratio depends only on the angle, which is why sin θ = y/r works on a circle of any size.

    Worked example

    A bicycle wheel has radius 0.35 m. The tire valve starts level with the hub on the right (3 o'clock). The wheel turns 150° counterclockwise. (a) Where is the valve relative to the hub? (b) How far did the valve travel along the rim?

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Convert the angle. 150° × π/180 = 5π/6 radians. It lands in quadrant II, with reference angle 30°.
    2. Height. On a circle of radius r the point is (r cos θ, r sin θ). y = 0.35 sin(5π/6) = 0.35 × 1/2 = 0.175 m above the hub.
    3. Width. x = 0.35 cos(5π/6) = 0.35 × (−√3/2) ≈ −0.303 m: 0.303 m to the left of the hub (the negative sign means left).
    4. (a) Answer. The valve is at (−0.303, 0.175) m relative to the hub: 0.303 m left and 0.175 m up.
    5. (b) Arc length. s = rθ = 0.35 × 5π/6 ≈ 0.916 m. The angle must be in radians for s = rθ.

    Worked example 2: exact values from the reference angle

    Find the exact values of sin(4π/3), cos(4π/3) and tan(4π/3).

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Locate the angle. 4π/3 = π + π/3: past the negative x-axis by π/3, so quadrant III.
    2. Reference angle. The acute angle to the x-axis is 4π/3 − π = π/3.
    3. Sizes from quadrant I. sin(π/3) = √3/2 and cos(π/3) = 1/2.
    4. Signs from the quadrant. In quadrant III both coordinates are negative: sin(4π/3) = −√3/2 and cos(4π/3) = −1/2.
    5. Tangent. tan = sin/cos = (−√3/2)/(−1/2) = √3. Positive, because the two negatives cancel (the radius slopes up to the right through the origin).

    Common mistakes

    • Mixing degrees and radians: sin(30) on a calculator in radian mode is sin of 30 radians, about −0.988, not 1/2.
    • Using the angle itself instead of the reference angle: sin(5π/6) is sin(π/6), not "sin of something bigger".
    • Getting the signs wrong: x is cosine (width) and y is sine (height). Quadrant II has negative cosine, positive sine.
    • Saying tan 90° = 0. It is undefined, because cos 90° = 0.
    • Using s = rθ with θ in degrees.

    Why the circle definition

    In a right triangle an angle can only be between 0° and 90°. Periodic things (a wheel, a tide, a sound wave) keep going around, so precalculus redefines sine and cosine as coordinates on the unit circle. For acute angles the two definitions agree: the radius is the hypotenuse (length 1), the height is the opposite side and the width is the adjacent side.

    Because the point is on the circle x² + y² = 1, every angle satisfies sin²θ + cos²θ = 1. That one fact is the Pythagorean theorem, and it gives one value from the other: if sin θ = 3/5 in quadrant II, then cos θ = −4/5.

    Check yourself: In which quadrant is sin θ < 0 and cos θ > 0?

    Sine & cosine graphs

    Unroll the unit circle: the height of the moving point is the sine wave, its width is the cosine wave.

    The idea

    Run a point around the unit circle and record its height at every angle: plotted against θ, that is y = sin θ. Record its width instead and you get y = cos θ. Both repeat every 2π, both stay between −1 and 1, and both have midline y = 0.

    Read the behavior straight off the circle. Going up the right side of the circle (θ from −π/2 to π/2) the height grows, so sin is increasing there; going down the left side it is decreasing. The width shrinks over the top half (0 to π), so cos is decreasing on (0, π) and increasing on (π, 2π).

    Near the top and bottom of the circle the point moves sideways, so the height barely changes: the sine wave flattens at its maximum and minimum. Near the sides it moves straight up or down: the sine wave is steepest where it crosses its midline. That is why sin is concave down above the midline and concave up below it.

    Symmetry: the angle −θ is the mirror image of θ across the x-axis. Same width, opposite height, so cos(−θ) = cos θ (cosine is even) and sin(−θ) = −sin θ (sine is odd).

    Assumption upgrade

    y = cos θ: widtheven: cos(−θ) = cos θ
    period 2πf(θ + 2π) = f(θ)
    range [−1, 1]amplitude 1, midline y = 0
