    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Press Play and watch the blue line carry the height across. At which angles is the height 0? At which is it biggest?

      What you should see

      Height 0 at θ = 0, π and 2π (the point is on the x-axis). The biggest height, 1, is at θ = π/2 (top of the circle); the smallest, −1, at 3π/2.

    2. Set θ = π/2 (1.571) and nudge it a little either way. Why does the sine graph look flat there?

      What you should see

      At the top of the circle the point is moving sideways, so its height hardly changes: sin θ stays near 1. The sine graph has a turning point there and is concave down.

    3. Trace cos only and drag θ from 0 to π. What happens to the width, and to the graph?

      What you should see

      The width falls from 1 to −1 as the point goes over the top of the circle, so cos is decreasing on (0, π). It falls fastest at θ = π/2, where the point moves straight left.

    4. In the second lab, set θ = 1 with sin, then switch to cos. Compare f(θ) and f(−θ) each time.

      What you should see

      sin(1) ≈ 0.841 and sin(−1) ≈ −0.841: opposite, so sine is odd (symmetric about the origin). cos(1) ≈ 0.540 and cos(−1) ≈ 0.540: equal, so cosine is even (symmetric about the y-axis).

    5. With sin, slide θ from 0 to 1.3 and watch the secant slope on [θ, θ + π/6]. What happens to the average rate?

      What you should see

      It shrinks from about 0.955 toward 0 and then turns negative: sine is increasing but more and more slowly, the signature of concave down. On [0, π/6] it is (1/2 − 0)/(π/6) = 3/π ≈ 0.955.

    Worked example

    On [0, 2π], find the interval where both sin θ and cos θ are decreasing. On that interval, describe the concavity of each graph.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Sine. The height falls as the point goes down the left side of the circle: sin is decreasing on (π/2, 3π/2).
    2. Cosine. The width falls as the point goes over the top: cos is decreasing on (0, π).
    3. Both. The overlap of (π/2, 3π/2) and (0, π) is (π/2, π): quadrant II.
    4. Concavity. On (π/2, π) sine is above its midline, so it is concave down: decreasing faster and faster. Cosine is below its midline there, so it is concave up: still decreasing, but more and more slowly.

    Worked example 2: a bicycle pedal

    A bicycle crank is 17 cm long and the pedal axle is 28 cm above the ground. With the crank horizontal and pointing forward at θ = 0, and θ measured counterclockwise as seen from the right side, the pedal's height is h(θ) = 28 + 17 sin θ cm. (a) Find the highest and lowest pedal heights. (b) Find h(7π/6). (c) On which interval of one turn is the pedal going down? (d) Compare the average rate of change of h on [0, π/6] and on [π/3, π/2].

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Model. The pedal is a point on a circle of radius 17 around the axle, so its height is the axle height plus 17 times the sine: h(θ) = 28 + 17 sin θ, midline 28.
    2. (a) sin θ is between −1 and 1, so h is between 28 − 17 = 11 cm (at θ = 3π/2) and 28 + 17 = 45 cm (at θ = π/2).
    3. (b) sin(7π/6) = −1/2, so h = 28 − 8.5 = 19.5 cm.
    4. (c) h decreases exactly where sin θ does: π/2 < θ < 3π/2, the half turn from the top to the bottom.
    5. (d) On [0, π/6]: (36.5 − 28)/(π/6) = 51/π ≈ 16.2 cm per radian. On [π/3, π/2]: 17(1 − √3/2)/(π/6) ≈ 4.35 cm per radian. Same angle turned, much less rise near the top: the graph is concave down there.

    Common mistakes

    • Swapping the two: sine is the height (y), cosine is the width (x).
    • Saying sin is increasing on (0, π). It increases only to π/2, then decreases.
    • Thinking the steepest part of a sine wave is at the max. The max is flat; the steepest part is at the midline.
    • Mixing up odd and even: cosine is even (the graph is symmetric about the y-axis), sine is odd.
    • Graphing with θ in degrees but labeling the axis in radians (or the other way around).

    Concavity without calculus

    Compare average rates of change over equal steps. For sin on [0, π/6], [π/6, π/3], [π/3, π/2] the rises are 0.5, 0.366 and 0.134: equal steps in θ, smaller and smaller rises. Decreasing rates of change mean concave down. Below the midline the rates increase, so the graph is concave up. The points of inflection are where the wave crosses its midline.

    Check yourself: On which interval is cos θ increasing?

    Sinusoidal transformations

    Every sine wave is the same wave, stretched and shifted. Four numbers say how: amplitude, period, phase shift and midline.

    The idea

    A sinusoidal function is any transformation of sine or cosine: f(θ) = a sin(b(θ + c)) + d. Each parameter does one job. a stretches vertically: the amplitude is |a|. d moves the wave up: the midline is y = d. b squeezes horizontally: the period is 2π/|b|. c slides it sideways: the phase shift is −c (so θ + π/4 moves the graph left by π/4).

    Cosine is a sine wave shifted left by π/2: cos θ = sin(θ + π/2). So a sinusoid can always be written either way; pick the one whose starting point is easiest (cosine starts at a maximum, sine starts on the midline going up).

    Read the parameters straight off a graph: midline = (max + min)/2, amplitude = (max − min)/2, period = the distance between two neighboring maxima.

    phase shift −cleft if c > 0
    frequency = |b|/2πcycles per unit

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Set a = 2, then a = −2. What does a negative a do?

      What you should see

      The amplitude is still 2, but the wave is flipped over its midline: it now starts on the midline going down. Amplitude is |a|.

    2. Set b = 2 and then b = 0.5 (keep a = 1). How long is one cycle each time?

      What you should see

      Period = 2π/b: π ≈ 3.14 for b = 2 (twice as many waves) and 4π ≈ 12.57 for b = 0.5 (half as many). Bigger b squeezes the wave.

    3. Set b = 2 and c = 0.785 (about π/4). Is the shift π/4 or π/8? Read the start of the cycle.

      What you should see

      π/4 to the left. The form b(θ + c) factors b out first, so the shift is −c = −π/4. Had it been written sin(2θ + π/4) = sin(2(θ + π/8)), the shift would be π/8.

    4. Choose cos with c = 0, then sin with c = 1.57. Compare the two graphs.

      What you should see

      They match (up to rounding of π/2): sin(θ + π/2) = cos θ. A cosine is a sine that starts half a hump early.

    5. In the second lab, drag the minimum farther right. What happens to the period?

      What you should see

      The period is twice the horizontal distance from a maximum to the next minimum. Doubling that distance doubles the period and halves b = 2π/period.

    Worked example

    Find the amplitude, period, phase shift, midline and range of f(θ) = 3 sin(2(θ − π/4)) + 1, then sketch one cycle.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Midline. d = 1, so the midline is y = 1.
    2. Amplitude. a = 3, so the wave rises 3 above and falls 3 below the midline: range [−2, 4].
    3. Period. b = 2, so the period is 2π/2 = π.
    4. Phase shift. θ − π/4 means c = −π/4: the cycle starts π/4 to the right, at θ = π/4, on the midline going up.
    5. Key points. A quarter period later (θ = π/4 + π/4 = π/2) it reaches the max 4; at θ = 3π/4 it is back on the midline; at θ = π it hits the min −2; at 5π/4 the cycle ends.

    Worked example 2: the voltage in a wall outlet

    The voltage of a US wall outlet is modeled by V(t) = 170 sin(120πt) volts, with t in seconds. (a) Find the amplitude, period and frequency. (b) When is the voltage first 85 V?

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Amplitude. a = 170: the voltage swings between −170 V and 170 V.
    2. Period and frequency. b = 120π, so the period is 2π/(120π) = 1/60 s and the frequency is 60 cycles per second (60 Hz).
    3. (b) Solve 170 sin(120πt) = 85. sin(120πt) = 1/2. The first positive angle with sine 1/2 is π/6, so 120πt = π/6 and t = 1/720 s ≈ 0.00139 s.
    4. Why "120 volts"? The label on an outlet is the root-mean-square value, peak ÷ √2: 170/√2 ≈ 120 V. The peak really is about 170 V (120√2 ≈ 169.7).

    Common mistakes

    • Reading the period as b instead of 2π/b.
    • Taking the phase shift from sin(2θ + π/2) as π/2. Factor first: sin(2(θ + π/4)), so the shift is π/4 to the left.
    • Getting the shift direction backwards: θ − h moves right by h, θ + h moves left.
    • Calling a negative a a negative amplitude. Amplitude is |a|; the sign flips the wave.
    • Forgetting the midline when finding max and min: max = d + |a|, min = d − |a|.

    Sine or cosine?

    Any sinusoid can be written with either. Cosine begins its cycle at a maximum, sine on the midline going up, so choose the one that matches an easy point on your graph or in your context. A Ferris wheel that starts at the bottom, for instance, is −cos: it starts at a minimum.

    Check yourself: What is the period of g(θ) = 4 cos(πθ/3) − 2?

    Check yourself: A sinusoid has a maximum of 9 and a minimum of 1. What are its midline and amplitude?

    AP Unit 3On the AP examCED 3.7

    Sinusoidal models

    Real data that rises and falls on a schedule can be modeled with a sinusoid. Read four numbers from the data and the model writes itself.

    The idea

    To model periodic data with f(t) = a cos(b(t − h)) + d, read the features straight from the data: the midline d = (max + min)/2, the amplitude |a| = (max − min)/2, the period P (so b = 2π/P), and the time of a maximum h (cosine starts at its maximum, so it is the natural choice). If it is easier to start at a minimum, use a = −|a|; if the data starts on the midline going up, use sine.

    A model is a simplification. Check it against the data: the vertical gaps between the data and the model (the residuals) should be small and show no pattern. A model is most trustworthy between the data points (interpolation) and over a few cycles; far outside the data the real situation can change.

    In context, every parameter has units and a meaning: d is the average level, |a| how far it swings, P how long one cycle takes, h when the peak happens. AP questions often ask you to interpret one of them or the value of the model at a time.

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose Daylight and press "Fit from the max and min". Read the four parameters. What does each mean here?

      What you should see

      d ≈ 12 hours (the average day), |a| ≈ 2.84 hours (the swing between summer and winter), P = 365 days (a year), and h ≈ 172 (June 21, the longest day).

    2. Still on daylight, change the period to 300 days. What happens to the residuals?

      What you should see

      They grow and show a pattern: the model drifts ahead of the data. A wrong period is the most damaging mistake, because the error builds up cycle after cycle.

    3. Choose Ferris wheel and fit. The data has small wiggles. Is the model wrong?

      What you should see

      No: real measurements have small errors. The residuals are tiny and patternless (RMS well under 1 m), so the sinusoid is a good model.

    4. In the second lab, switch between the three starting positions. Which form of the equation is simplest for each?

      What you should see

      Bottom: h = c − r cos(2πt/T), a cosine flipped. 3 o'clock rising: h = c + r sin(2πt/T). Top: h = c + r cos(2πt/T). Same wheel, three simplest equations.

    5. Set radius 40, center 80, time for one turn 2 (a wind turbine scale, but in minutes). Press Play. When is the tip highest?

      What you should see

      Starting at 3 o'clock rising, the tip reaches the top a quarter turn later: t = 0.5 min, at 120 m.

    Worked example: hours of daylight

    The table gives the hours of daylight at 40° N latitude on the 21st of each month (day 21, 52, 80, …, 355). The longest is 14.84 h on day 172 (June 21) and the shortest is 9.16 h on day 355 (December 21). Build a sinusoidal model, then use it to estimate how many days per year have more than 14 hours of daylight.

    Daylight at 40° N
    day215280111141172202233264294325355
    hours9.6110.7211.9513.3214.3914.8414.4313.3411.9810.669.579.16

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Max and min. 14.84 h at day 172 and 9.16 h at day 355.
    2. Midline and amplitude. d = (14.84 + 9.16)/2 = 12 and |a| = (14.84 − 9.16)/2 = 2.84.
    3. Period. The cycle is one year: P = 365 days, so b = 2π/365. (Check: max to min is 183 days, about half a year.)
    4. Model. Start at the maximum with cosine: D(t) = 12 + 2.84 cos(2π(t − 172)/365).
    5. More than 14 h. 2.84 cos(…) > 2 gives cos(2π(t − 172)/365) > 0.704, so |t − 172| < (365/2π)·arccos(0.704) ≈ 45.9. That is day 126 to day 218 (about May 6 to August 6): about 92 days. The sun's actual position gives 87 days: close, but a reminder that the model is an approximation.

    Worked example 2: a wind turbine blade

    A wind turbine's hub is 80 m above the ground and each blade is 40 m long. The rotor turns once every 4 seconds. At t = 0 a blade tip is level with the hub and rising. (a) Write h(t), the tip's height. (b) Find h(1.5). (c) For how long during each turn is the tip above 100 m?

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Features. Midline = hub height 80 m; amplitude = blade length 40 m; period 4 s, so b = 2π/4 = π/2.
    2. (a) Which function? It starts on the midline going up, so use sine: h(t) = 80 + 40 sin(πt/2).
    3. Check. At t = 1 (a quarter turn) h = 80 + 40 = 120 m, the top. ✓
    4. (b) h(1.5) = 80 + 40 sin(3π/4) = 80 + 20√2 ≈ 108.3 m.
    5. (c) 80 + 40 sin(πt/2) > 100 gives sin(πt/2) > 1/2, so π/6 < πt/2 < 5π/6 and 1/3 < t < 5/3. That is 4/3 s of every 4-second turn: one third of the time.

    Common mistakes

    • Using the period itself as b. b = 2π/P.
    • Reading the midline as the starting value. It is (max + min)/2.
    • Using sine when the data starts at a maximum, then fighting with a phase shift. Pick the function whose starting point matches.
    • Judging a fit by one point. Look at all the residuals: small and patternless is the goal.
    • Trusting the model far beyond the data (decades of daylight is fine; decades of stock prices is not).

    Why cosine is usually easier for data

    Data tables almost always show the maximum and the minimum clearly; the midline crossing is between data points and harder to pin down. Cosine with a = +|a| starts at a maximum, so the phase h is just "when is it biggest". If the minimum is clearer, use −cos and the time of the minimum.

    Check yourself: Temperatures in a city peak at 30 °C in late July and bottom out at 2 °C in late January. What is the amplitude of a sinusoidal model?

    Check yourself: In h(t) = 15 − 12 cos(πt/20), t in seconds, what is the period?

    AP Unit 3On the AP examCED 3.8

    The tangent function

    Tangent is the slope of the radius. It repeats every half turn and shoots off to infinity whenever the radius stands straight up.

    The idea

    On the unit circle the radius to the angle θ runs from (0, 0) to (cos θ, sin θ), so its slope is tan θ = sin θ / cos θ. Extend the radius until it hits the vertical line x = 1: it hits at height tan θ. That segment is where the name "tangent" comes from.

    When the radius is vertical (θ = π/2, 3π/2, ...) cos θ = 0 and the slope is undefined: the graph has a vertical asymptote. Between two asymptotes the slope runs through every real number, from −∞ to ∞, and it is increasing the whole way.

    Turning the radius by half a turn (π) points it the opposite way, but a line through the origin has the same slope in both directions, so tan(θ + π) = tan θ: the period is π, not 2π. Transformations work as for sine: f(θ) = a tan(b(θ + c)) + d has period π/|b|.

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Drag θ from 0 toward π/2 (1.571). What happens to the orange tangent segment and to tan θ?

      What you should see

      The radius gets steeper, the segment on x = 1 climbs faster and faster, and tan θ grows without bound: tan 1.3 ≈ 3.6, tan 1.5 ≈ 14.1. At π/2 it is undefined.

    2. Go just past π/2, to about 1.65. Where is the tangent segment now?

      What you should see

      Far below the axis: tan 1.65 ≈ −12.6. The radius now slopes down to the right when extended backward through the origin to x = 1. The graph jumps from +∞ to −∞ across the asymptote.

    3. Set θ = 0.5, then θ = 0.5 + π ≈ 3.64. Compare the values.

      What you should see

      Both are ≈ 0.546. The two radii point opposite ways along the same line through the origin, so they have the same slope: the period of tangent is π.

    4. In the second lab set b = 2. Where are the asymptotes now, and what is the period?

      What you should see

      tan(2θ) is undefined when 2θ = π/2 + kπ, so θ = π/4 + kπ/2: every π/2. The period is π/2, half the parent period.

    5. Set a = −1 (b = 1). Is the graph still increasing between asymptotes?

      What you should see

      No: a negative a flips it, so each branch is decreasing. The asymptotes and the period do not change.

    Worked example

    For g(θ) = 3 tan(θ/2) + 1, find the period and the vertical asymptotes, and evaluate g(π/2) and g(−π/2).

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Asymptotes. tan(θ/2) is undefined when θ/2 = π/2 + kπ, so θ = π + 2kπ: …, −π, π, 3π, …
    2. Period. b = 1/2, so the period is π ÷ (1/2) = 2π: the distance between neighboring asymptotes.
    3. Center of a branch. At θ = 0, tan 0 = 0 and g(0) = 1. Each branch passes through its center on the line y = 1 (the d value).
    4. Values. g(π/2) = 3 tan(π/4) + 1 = 3 + 1 = 4, and g(−π/2) = 3 tan(−π/4) + 1 = −3 + 1 = −2. Since a = 3 > 0, each branch increases from −∞ to ∞.

    Worked example 2: tracking a rocket

    A camera on the ground 50 m from a launch pad tilts up to follow a rocket rising straight up. When the camera's angle of elevation is θ, the rocket's height is h = 50 tan θ meters. (a) Find h at θ = π/6, π/4 and π/3. (b) Find the average rate of change of h on [π/6, π/4] and on [π/4, π/3]. (c) What happens as θ approaches π/2?

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Model. In the right triangle, the side opposite θ is the height h and the side adjacent is 50 m, so tan θ = h/50 and h = 50 tan θ.
    2. (a) h(π/6) = 50 · √3/3 ≈ 28.87 m; h(π/4) = 50 · 1 = 50 m; h(π/3) = 50√3 ≈ 86.60 m.
    3. (b) (50 − 28.87)/(π/12) ≈ 80.7 m per radian, then (86.60 − 50)/(π/12) ≈ 139.8 m per radian. Equal turns of the camera cover more and more height: h is concave up on (0, π/2).
    4. (c) As θ → π/2, cos θ → 0 and tan θ → ∞. At 80° the rocket is 283.6 m up, at 85° it is 571.5 m. The camera never points straight up: θ = π/2 is a vertical asymptote.

    Common mistakes

    • Using period 2π for tangent. It is π (or π/|b| after a squeeze).
    • Putting asymptotes where sin θ = 0. Those are the zeros; the asymptotes are where cos θ = 0.
    • Evaluating tan(π/2) as 0 or 1. It is undefined.
    • Thinking a tangent graph has a maximum. Each branch goes from −∞ to ∞ (or the reverse).
    • Forgetting that the period of a tan(bθ) is π/|b|, not 2π/|b|.

    Why the period is π

    Sine and cosine come back to the same value only after a full turn, because the point must return to the same place. Tangent only needs the same slope, and the radius at θ + π lies along the same line as the radius at θ (pointing the opposite way). Algebraically, sin(θ + π) = −sin θ and cos(θ + π) = −cos θ, and the two negatives cancel in the ratio.

    Check yourself: What is the period of f(θ) = 2 tan(3θ)?

    Check yourself: Where does y = tan θ have a vertical asymptote?

    AP Unit 3On the AP examCED 3.9

    Inverse trig functions

    Ask the question backwards: which angle has this sine? Infinitely many do, so each inverse function agrees to give just one.

    The idea

    Sine takes an angle and gives a height. The inverse question, "which angle has height 1/2?", has infinitely many answers (π/6, 5π/6, π/6 + 2π, ...). A function must give one output, so we restrict the domain of sine to an interval where it is one-to-one and takes every value once: [−π/2, π/2], the right half of the circle. On that piece, the inverse is arcsin (also written sin⁻¹).

    The same idea for the others: cosine is restricted to [0, π] (the top half), giving arccos; tangent to (−π/2, π/2), giving arctan. So arcsin and arctan always answer between −π/2 and π/2, and arccos always answers between 0 and π.

    The graph of an inverse is the graph of the restricted function reflected over the line y = x: inputs and outputs trade places. arcsin and arccos take inputs only from [−1, 1] (heights and widths on the unit circle); arctan takes any real number (any slope).

    θ = arccos x ⇔ cos θ = xθ in [0, π]
    θ = arctan x ⇔ tan θ = xθ in (−π/2, π/2)

    Pick the one the function gives: 11 values

    Each inverse gives one angle, from its gold range. Find the direction first, then the angle in the range.

    1. arcsin(1/2) = ?

    Height 1/2 happens at π/6 and 5π/6, but arcsin only answers on the right half of the circle (−π/2 to π/2). So π/6.

    2. arcsin(−√2/2) = ?

    7π/4 points the right way, but it is outside [−π/2, π/2]. The same direction inside the allowed range is −π/4.

    3. arccos(−1/2) = ?

    Width −1/2 happens at 2π/3 and 4π/3. arccos only answers on the top half (0 to π), so 2π/3.

    4. arccos(√3/2) = ?

    Width √3/2 on the top half is at π/6. (−π/6 has the same width but is on the bottom half.)

    5. arctan(−1) = ?

    Slope −1 at 3π/4 and at −π/4 (the same line). arctan answers on the right half, open interval (−π/2, π/2): −π/4.

    6. arctan(√3) = ?

    Slope √3 = sin/cos = (√3/2)/(1/2): the angle π/3. 4π/3 lies on the same line but outside the range.

    7. arcsin(−1) = ?

    Height −1 is the bottom of the circle. In [−π/2, π/2] that angle is −π/2, not 3π/2.

    8. arccos(0) = ?

    Width 0 on the top half: straight up, π/2.

    9. arccos(−√2/2) = ?

    Width −√2/2 on the top half is in quadrant II: 3π/4.

    10. arcsin(sin(5π/6)) = ?

    sin(5π/6) = 1/2, so this is arcsin(1/2) = π/6. arcsin cannot return 5π/6: it is outside [−π/2, π/2]. "arcsin undoes sin" only on that range.

    11. arctan(−√3/3) = ?

    Slope −√3/3 = −tan(π/6). In (−π/2, π/2): −π/6.

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. With arcsin, set x = 0.87 (it snaps to √3/2). Read the output, then find the matching point on the blue sine graph.

      What you should see

      arcsin(√3/2) = π/3 ≈ 1.047. The blue point (π/3, √3/2) on the sine graph and the green point (√3/2, π/3) on the arcsin graph are mirror images across y = x: input and output trade places.

    2. Tick "Show the whole unrestricted graph". Why can't the whole sine wave be flipped?

      What you should see

      Flipped, the full wave would fail the vertical line test: one x would go to many angles. Only the solid piece on [−π/2, π/2] passes the horizontal line test, so only it has an inverse function.

    3. Switch to arccos and set x = −0.5. Is the answer negative?

      What you should see

      No: arccos(−0.5) = 2π/3 ≈ 2.094. arccos answers on the top half of the circle, [0, π], so its outputs are never negative. A negative input means an angle in quadrant II.

    4. In the second lab choose sin and k = 0.5. How many angles in view have sine 0.5? Which does arcsin pick?

      What you should see

      Four in [−2π, 2π] (−11π/6, −7π/6, π/6, 5π/6), and infinitely many overall. arcsin picks π/6, the one on the gold restricted piece.

    5. Choose tan and push k to 4, then −4. Does arctan ever reach π/2?

      What you should see

      No. arctan 4 ≈ 1.326 and arctan(−4) ≈ −1.326. As k grows the answer creeps toward π/2 ≈ 1.571 but never gets there: y = ±π/2 are horizontal asymptotes of arctan.

    Worked example

    Evaluate exactly: (a) arccos(−1/2) (b) arcsin(sin(3π/4)) (c) cos(arcsin(3/5)).

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. (a) Range first. arccos answers in [0, π], the top half of the circle.
    2. (a) Find the angle. Width −1/2 on the top half is in quadrant II with reference angle π/3: arccos(−1/2) = 2π/3.
    3. (a) Check. cos(2π/3) = −1/2 and 2π/3 is in [0, π]. ✓
    4. (b) sin(3π/4) = √2/2. arcsin(√2/2) must be in [−π/2, π/2], so it is π/4, not 3π/4. The inverse undoes sine only on its restricted range.
    5. (c) Let θ = arcsin(3/5): sin θ = 3/5 with θ in quadrant I. On a 3-4-5 right triangle (or from sin² + cos² = 1), cos θ = √(1 − 9/25) = 4/5, positive because θ is in [−π/2, π/2].

    Worked example 2: ladders and ramps

    A 6 m ladder leans against a wall with its foot 1.5 m from the wall. (a) Find the angle θ between the ladder and the ground. (b) A wheelchair ramp rises 0.5 m over a horizontal run of 6 m. Find its angle with the ground.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Set up (a). The ladder is the hypotenuse (6 m) and the distance along the ground is the side adjacent to θ (1.5 m), so cos θ = 1.5/6 = 0.25.
    2. Which inverse? We know a cosine and want the angle, so θ = arccos(0.25). An acute angle is in arccos's range [0, π], so this is the one we want.
    3. (a) Answer. θ = arccos(0.25) ≈ 1.318 rad ≈ 75.5°. This is the "4 to 1" ladder safety rule: the foot one quarter of the ladder's length from the wall.
    4. (b) Rise over run is the tangent: tan θ = 0.5/6 = 1/12, so θ = arctan(1/12) ≈ 0.0831 rad ≈ 4.76°. A 1 : 12 slope is the steepest ramp the US accessibility standards allow.

    Common mistakes

    • Answering arcsin(1/2) = 5π/6 or 150°. Both have sine 1/2, but arcsin only returns angles in [−π/2, π/2].
    • Giving a negative answer for arccos. Its range is [0, π].
    • Assuming arcsin(sin θ) = θ always. It is true only when θ is in [−π/2, π/2].
    • Reading sin⁻¹ x as 1/sin x. The −1 means inverse function, not reciprocal; 1/sin x is csc x.
    • Taking arcsin of a number bigger than 1. No angle has sine 1.2: it is not in the domain.

    Why these ranges

    Each range is chosen to contain the acute angles (so right-triangle problems work directly), to hit every output value exactly once, and to be one connected piece. For sine that is [−π/2, π/2]: from the bottom of the circle up the right side to the top. For cosine it is [0, π], the top half, because the right half would give each width twice.

    Check yourself: What is arctan(−1)?

    Check yourself: What is arccos(cos(−π/3))?

    AP Unit 3On the AP examCED 3.10

    Trig equations & inequalities

    Solving a trig equation means finding where a wave meets a horizontal line: find every crossing in one period, then add whole periods.

    The idea

    To solve sin θ = k, isolate the trig function first, then picture the line y = k crossing the wave (or the horizontal line at height k crossing the unit circle). For −1 < k < 1 it crosses twice per period; at k = ±1 it touches once; for |k| > 1 there is no solution.

    Find the two angles in [0, 2π) with the reference angle and the quadrant signs. Then the general solution adds whole periods: θ = θ₁ + 2πk and θ = θ₂ + 2πk for sine and cosine, θ = θ₁ + πk for tangent. The inverse function gives one solution; the picture gives the rest.

    For an inequality like sin θ > k, the solutions of the equation are the boundaries. Between them, the wave is either above the line or below it: test one point, or just look. With an inside factor, as in sin(2θ) = k, solve for 2θ over the stretched interval [0, 4π) first, then divide.

    Where does the line cross? 8 equations

    Each equation is a horizontal line meeting a wave. Predict the crossings, then check.

    1. Solve sin θ = 1/2 on [0, 2π).

    Height 1/2: π/6 in quadrant I and its mirror π − π/6 = 5π/6 in quadrant II, where sine is also positive.

    2. Solve cos θ = −√2/2 on [0, 2π).

    Width −√2/2: quadrants II and III (cosine negative), reference angle π/4: 3π/4 and 5π/4.

    3. Solve tan θ = 1 on [0, 2π).

    Tangent repeats every π: π/4 and π/4 + π = 5π/4.

    4. Solve sin θ = −1 on [0, 2π).

    The line y = −1 just touches the bottom of the wave once per period: θ = 3π/2.

    5. Solve 2 cos θ − 1 = 0 on [0, 2π).

    Isolate first: cos θ = 1/2. Quadrants I and IV: π/3 and 2π − π/3 = 5π/3.

    6. Solve sin(2θ) = 0 on [0, 2π).

    sin(2θ) completes two cycles in [0, 2π), so twice as many zeros: 2θ = 0, π, 2π, 3π gives θ = 0, π/2, π, 3π/2.

    7. Solve cos θ = 2 on [0, 2π).

    The line y = 2 never meets the cosine wave: cosine never exceeds 1. No solution.

    8. Solve tan θ = −√3 on [0, 2π).

    Slope −√3: reference angle π/3 in quadrants II and IV, where tangent is negative: 2π/3 and 5π/3 (π apart).

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Solve sin θ = 1/2: set k = 0.5. Where are the two solutions on the circle?

      What you should see

      π/6 and 5π/6: the horizontal line at height 1/2 cuts the circle in quadrants I and II, mirror images across the y-axis.

    2. Switch to cos with k = 0.5. Why are the solutions now in quadrants I and IV?

      What you should see

      Cosine is the width, so the line is vertical, x = 1/2. It cuts the circle at π/3 and 5π/3, mirror images across the x-axis.

    3. Choose sin and "f(θ) > k" with k = −0.5. Read the shaded intervals.

      What you should see

      [0, 7π/6) ∪ (11π/6, 2π): everywhere except the bottom stretch of the circle where the height dips below −1/2.

    4. Choose tan with k = 1. How many solutions in [0, 2π), and how far apart?

      What you should see

      Two, π/4 and 5π/4, exactly π apart: the period of tangent. The line y = x through the origin cuts the circle at both.

    5. In the second lab set k = 0.5 and step b from 1 to 4. Count the solutions.

      What you should see

      2, 4, 6, 8: sin(bθ) runs through b full cycles in [0, 2π), and each cycle meets the line twice.

    Worked example

    Solve 2 sin θ + 1 = 0 on [0, 2π), give the general solution, then solve 2 sin θ + 1 > 0 on [0, 2π).

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Isolate. 2 sin θ = −1, so sin θ = −1/2.
    2. Reference angle and quadrants. |−1/2| = sin(π/6), so the reference angle is π/6. Sine is negative in quadrants III and IV: θ = π + π/6 = 7π/6…
    3. …and θ = 2π − π/6 = 11π/6. General solution: θ = 7π/6 + 2πk or θ = 11π/6 + 2πk, for any integer k.
    4. Inequality. sin θ > −1/2 everywhere the wave is above the line: [0, 7π/6) ∪ (11π/6, 2π). Check θ = 0: 2(0) + 1 = 1 > 0 ✓.

    Worked example 2: when can the boat leave?

    In a simplified model, the depth of water at a harbor entrance is h(t) = 3 + 1.5 cos(πt/6) meters, t hours after high tide. A boat needs at least 3.75 m of water. During which times in the first 12 hours can it pass?

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Inequality. 3 + 1.5 cos(πt/6) ≥ 3.75.
    2. Isolate. 1.5 cos(πt/6) ≥ 0.75, so cos(πt/6) ≥ 1/2. Let u = πt/6; for 0 ≤ t ≤ 12, u runs over [0, 2π].
    3. Boundaries. cos u = 1/2 at u = π/3 and u = 5π/3, so t = 6u/π = 2 and 10 hours.
    4. Which side? cos u ≥ 1/2 near u = 0 (width close to 1): u in [0, π/3] or [5π/3, 2π]. So 0 ≤ t ≤ 2 and 10 ≤ t ≤ 12: the 2 hours on either side of high tide, 4 hours of every 12.

    Common mistakes

    • Stopping at the one answer the calculator gives. arcsin(−1/2) = −π/6 is not even in [0, 2π); the two answers are 7π/6 and 11π/6.
    • Dividing by the trig function and losing solutions: in sin θ cos θ = sin θ, factor (sin θ(cos θ − 1) = 0) instead of dividing by sin θ.
    • Forgetting to solve for the inside: for sin(2θ) = 1/2, solve for 2θ on [0, 4π), then divide by 2.
    • Using + 2πk for tangent. Its period is π, so θ = θ₁ + πk.
    • Getting the inequality backwards: check one test point.

    Why there are two solutions per period

    A horizontal line at height k (with −1 < k < 1) cuts the unit circle in two points, mirror images across the y-axis: θ and π − θ. A vertical line at width k cuts it in two points mirrored across the x-axis: θ and −θ (or 2π − θ). That is the whole reason behind the formulas θ₂ = π − θ₁ for sine and θ₂ = 2π − θ₁ for cosine.

    Check yourself: How many solutions does cos θ = −0.3 have in [0, 2π)?

    Check yourself: Which is the general solution of tan θ = √3?

    AP Unit 3On the AP examCED 3.11

    Secant, cosecant & cotangent

    Flip each trig function upside down and you get three more. Small values become huge, and every zero becomes an asymptote.

    The idea

    The reciprocal trig functions are sec θ = 1/cos θ, csc θ = 1/sin θ and cot θ = 1/tan θ = cos θ / sin θ. Each is undefined exactly where the function it flips is zero, which gives a vertical asymptote.

    Flipping a number keeps its sign and swaps big and small: 1/0.5 = 2 and 1/(−0.1) = −10. Since sine and cosine stay between −1 and 1, secant and cosecant are never between −1 and 1: |sec θ| ≥ 1 and |csc θ| ≥ 1. Where the parent touches ±1, the reciprocal touches ±1 too (the U-shaped branches turn around there).

    They have lengths on the unit circle: draw the tangent line at (1, 0). The radius extended meets it at height tan θ, and the distance from the origin to that point is |sec θ|. On the horizontal tangent line y = 1 the same trick gives cot θ and |csc θ|.

    csc θ = 1 / sin θasymptotes where sin θ = 0

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose sec θ and drag θ to 0. Why is sec 0 = 1, and why is the secant graph at its lowest positive value there?

      What you should see

      cos 0 = 1 is the biggest cosine can be, so its reciprocal 1/1 = 1 is the smallest positive secant. On the circle, the sec segment is just the radius along the x-axis: length 1.

    2. Slide θ toward π/2 (1.571). What happens to cos θ, sec θ and the orange sec segment?

      What you should see

      cos θ shrinks toward 0, so sec θ = 1/cos θ blows up. The radius line meets x = 1 farther and farther up, and at π/2 it never meets it: an asymptote.

    3. Choose csc θ and set θ = 7π/6 (3.665). Predict the sign and value.

      What you should see

      sin(7π/6) = −1/2, so csc(7π/6) = −2. Negative, because the reciprocal keeps the sign.

    4. Choose cot θ. Where are its asymptotes, compared with tan θ?

      What you should see

      cot θ is undefined where sin θ = 0: θ = 0, π, 2π. Those are exactly the zeros of tan θ, and cot θ is zero where tan θ has asymptotes (π/2, 3π/2).

    5. In the second lab, set a = 2. How close to 0 does the reciprocal get now?

      What you should see

      The wave reaches ±2, so the reciprocal reaches ±1/2 and never gets closer to 0. A taller wave gives a flatter reciprocal.

    Worked example

    Find the exact values of sec(2π/3), csc(2π/3) and cot(2π/3).

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. The point. 2π/3 is in quadrant II with reference angle π/3: (cos, sin) = (−1/2, √3/2).
    2. Secant. sec(2π/3) = 1/cos(2π/3) = 1/(−1/2) = −2.
    3. Cosecant. csc(2π/3) = 1/(√3/2) = 2/√3 = 2√3/3 ≈ 1.155.
    4. Cotangent. cot(2π/3) = cos/sin = (−1/2)/(√3/2) = −1/√3 = −√3/3 ≈ −0.577. Check: tan(2π/3) = −√3, and 1/(−√3) = −√3/3 ✓.

    Worked example 2: a lighthouse beam

    A lighthouse stands 2 km from a straight shoreline. Its beam makes an angle θ with the line straight out to the shore. (a) Show that the beam travels d = 2 sec θ km to reach the shore and the lit spot is x = 2 tan θ km along the shore. (b) Find d and x at θ = π/3. (c) What happens as θ → π/2?

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Right triangle. The side adjacent to θ is the 2 km to the shore. The beam is the hypotenuse d, so cos θ = 2/d and d = 2/cos θ = 2 sec θ.
    2. Along the shore. The opposite side is x, so tan θ = x/2 and x = 2 tan θ.
    3. (b) θ = π/3: sec(π/3) = 1/(1/2) = 2, so d = 4 km; tan(π/3) = √3, so x = 2√3 ≈ 3.46 km.
    4. (c) As θ → π/2, cos θ → 0, so sec θ → ∞: the beam nearly parallels the shore and the spot runs off without bound. θ = π/2 is a vertical asymptote of both d and x.

    Common mistakes

    • Writing sec θ = 1/sin θ. The "co" functions pair up: cosecant goes with sine, secant with cosine.
    • Confusing sec θ with arccos θ (cos⁻¹ θ). One is a reciprocal, the other an inverse.
    • Putting the asymptotes of sec θ where sin θ = 0. They are where cos θ = 0.
    • Expecting sec θ = 0 somewhere. A reciprocal is never 0.
    • Forgetting the sign: csc θ is negative wherever sin θ is.

    Reading a reciprocal graph from its parent

    Sketch the parent lightly. Draw a vertical asymptote at each zero. Where the parent is ±1, plot ±1. Then, between asymptotes, the reciprocal is on the same side of the axis as the parent and gets farther from the axis where the parent gets closer: each hump of the sine wave turns into a U opening away from the axis.

    Check yourself: What is csc(π/6)?

    Check yourself: Which is in the range of y = sec θ?

    AP Unit 3On the AP examCED 3.12

    Identities & equivalent forms

    The same function can wear many different formulas. Identities let you swap one for another to simplify, evaluate or solve.

    The idea

    An identity is an equation that is true for every input where both sides are defined. Graphically, the two sides have exactly the same graph. The most important one is the unit circle itself: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1. Divide it by cos²θ or sin²θ and you get 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ and 1 + cot²θ = csc²θ.

    The sum and difference formulas give the trig values of combined angles: sin(α ± β) = sin α cos β ± cos α sin β and cos(α ± β) = cos α cos β ∓ sin α sin β. Note that sin(α + β) is not sin α + sin β. Setting β = α gives the double-angle formulas: sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ and cos 2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ = 1 − 2 sin²θ = 2 cos²θ − 1.

    Identities are tools. Use them to find exact values (sin 75° = sin(45° + 30°)), to rewrite an expression into one trig function before solving an equation, and to turn a product or a square into a sum, which is easier to graph and interpret.

    Assumption upgrade

    Before

    Now
    equations often mix sin, cos, squares and double angles
    So we need
    the Pythagorean, sum and difference, and double-angle identities, and how to use them

    cos(α ± β) = cos α cos β ∓ sin α sin β

    Same graph, different name: 10 identities

    Two expressions are identical when their graphs match everywhere. Predict, then see the match.

    1. Which expression is identical to 1 − cos²θ?

    sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, so 1 − cos²θ = sin²θ.

    2. Which expression is identical to 2 sin θ cos θ?

    The double-angle formula: sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ. The graph has period π.

    3. Which expression is identical to cos²θ − sin²θ?

    cos 2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ. (The Pythagorean identity would give 1 only for cos² + sin².)

    4. Which expression is identical to sin(θ + π/2)?

    Shifting sine left by π/2 gives cosine: sin(θ + π/2) = sin θ cos(π/2) + cos θ sin(π/2) = cos θ.

    5. Which expression is identical to cos(θ − π)?

    cos(θ − π) = cos θ cos π + sin θ sin π = −cos θ. Half a turn flips the point to the opposite side.

    6. Which expression is identical to tan θ cos θ?

    tan θ cos θ = (sin θ / cos θ) cos θ = sin θ, wherever cos θ ≠ 0 (the graph has holes there).

    7. Which expression is identical to 1 + cot²θ?

    Divide sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 by sin²θ: 1 + cot²θ = csc²θ.

    8. Which expression is identical to cos(π/2 − θ)?

    Cofunction identity: cos(π/2 − θ) = sin θ. The "co" in cosine means "sine of the complement".

    9. Which expression is identical to sin 2θ / (2 cos θ)?

    sin 2θ / (2 cos θ) = 2 sin θ cos θ / (2 cos θ) = sin θ (with holes where cos θ = 0).

    10. Which expression is identical to sec²θ − tan²θ?

    From 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ: sec²θ − tan²θ = 1, a flat line with holes at the asymptotes of tan.

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose sin² + cos² and slide θ. Does the orange line ever leave the blue curve?

      What you should see

      Never: the left side is always exactly 1, a flat line. Every point (cos θ, sin θ) is on the circle of radius 1.

    2. Choose sin 2θ. Compare 2 sin θ cos θ with 2 sin θ at θ = 1.

      What you should see

      sin 2 ≈ 0.909 and 2 sin 1 cos 1 ≈ 0.909 agree; 2 sin 1 ≈ 1.683 does not. Doubling the angle is not doubling the sine.

    3. Choose sin(θ + β) vs sin θ + sin β. Set β = 0.79 (about π/4). Are the curves the same?

      What you should see

      No: sin θ + sin β reaches 1.71 but sin(θ + β) never exceeds 1. Sine does not distribute over addition: sin(α + β) ≠ sin α + sin β.

    4. In the second lab choose Squares on the legs. Drag θ. What do the two square areas add up to?

      What you should see

      Always 1, the area of the square on the hypotenuse (the radius). That is the Pythagorean theorem, and it is sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.

    5. Choose Adding two angles with α = 0.79 and β = 0.52 (about π/4 and π/6). Compare the two ways of computing sin(α + β).

      What you should see

      Directly, sin(1.31) ≈ 0.966. By the formula, sin α cos β + cos α sin β ≈ 0.707(0.866) + 0.707(0.5) ≈ 0.966. That is sin 75° = (√6 + √2)/4.

    Worked example

    sin θ = 3/5 and θ is in quadrant II. Find cos θ, tan θ, sin 2θ and cos 2θ exactly.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Picture. Height 3/5 on the unit circle, on the left side (quadrant II).
    2. Pythagorean identity. cos²θ = 1 − sin²θ = 1 − 9/25 = 16/25, so cos θ = ±4/5. In quadrant II cosine is negative: cos θ = −4/5.
    3. Tangent. tan θ = (3/5)/(−4/5) = −3/4.
    4. Double angle. sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ = 2(3/5)(−4/5) = −24/25.
    5. And cos 2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ = 16/25 − 9/25 = 7/25. Check: (−24/25)² + (7/25)² = (576 + 49)/625 = 1 ✓.

    Worked example 2: power from a wall outlet

    A space heater element on a US outlet draws power p(t) = 340 sin²(120πt) watts, t in seconds. Use an identity to rewrite p(t) as a sinusoid. What is the average power, and how often does the power repeat?

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. The problem. A squared sine is not in a sinusoid form a cos(bt) + d, so its midline and period are hard to read.
    2. Identity. From cos 2x = 1 − 2 sin²x: sin²x = (1 − cos 2x)/2.
    3. Rewrite. p(t) = 340 · (1 − cos(240πt))/2 = 170 − 170 cos(240πt). Now it is a sinusoid with midline 170 and amplitude 170.
    4. Read it. The average (midline) is 170 W, half the peak. The period is 2π/(240π) = 1/120 s: the power pulses 120 times a second, twice per voltage cycle, because it is the same whether the current flows one way or the other.

    Common mistakes

    • Writing sin(α + β) = sin α + sin β, or sin 2θ = 2 sin θ.
    • Choosing the wrong sign after a square root: use the quadrant to decide.
    • Confusing sin²θ (the square of sin θ) with sin(θ²).
    • Dividing both sides of an equation by sin θ and losing the solutions where sin θ = 0. Factor instead.
    • Using the wrong form of cos 2θ: pick the one that matches what you know (1 − 2 sin²θ when you know sin θ).

    Solving with identities

    To solve cos 2θ = cos θ on [0, 2π), rewrite with one function: 2cos²θ − 1 = cos θ, so 2cos²θ − cos θ − 1 = 0, which factors as (2 cos θ + 1)(cos θ − 1) = 0. Then cos θ = −1/2 (θ = 2π/3, 4π/3) or cos θ = 1 (θ = 0). The identity turned a double-angle equation into a quadratic in cos θ.

    Check yourself: Which is equal to sin θ cos θ?

    Check yourself: What is the exact value of cos 15° = cos(45° − 30°)?

    AP Unit 3On the AP examCED 3.13

    Polar coordinates

    Instead of "over and up", say "how far and which way". A point in the plane can be named by its distance from the origin and its angle.

    The idea

    In polar coordinates a point is (r, θ): turn to the angle θ (counterclockwise from the positive x-axis), then go a distance r along that ray. It is how radar, sonar and a lighthouse beam describe position.

    Converting is the unit circle again, scaled by r: x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ. Going back, r² = x² + y² and tan θ = y/x, but tan θ = y/x has two solutions in each full turn: choose the angle in the quadrant where the point actually is.

    One point has many polar names. Adding 2π to θ lands on the same ray. A negative r means "walk backwards": (−r, θ) is the same point as (r, θ + π). A complex number a + bi is the point (a, b), so it has a polar form too: a + bi = r(cos θ + i sin θ).

    every point had exactly one name, (x, y)
    So we didn't need

    Now

    So we need

    r² = x² + y² · tan θ = y/xrectangular → polar

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Set r = 3 and θ = 135°. Predict (x, y) before you read it.

      What you should see

      x = 3 cos 135° = −3√2/2 ≈ −2.121 and y = 3 sin 135° ≈ 2.121: the point is up and to the left, as quadrant II should be.

    2. Keep r = 3, θ = 135° and tick "negative r". Where does the point go?

      What you should see

      To (2.121, −2.121), on the opposite ray (315°). (−3, 135°) is the same point as (3, 315°): a negative r walks backwards.

    3. Set θ = 30°, then 390° would be... why does the slider stop at 360°?

      What you should see

      Because 390° is the same ray as 30°. Every point has infinitely many polar names: (2, 30°) = (2, 390°) = (2, −330°) = (−2, 210°).

    4. In the complex plane set a = 1, b = 1.7 (about √3). Read r and θ.

      What you should see

      r = √(1 + 1.7²) ≈ 1.97 and θ ≈ 59.5°. With b = √3 exactly it is r = 2, θ = π/3: 1 + i√3 = 2(cos π/3 + i sin π/3).

    5. Set a = −2, b = 0. What is θ, and why is "θ = arctan(b/a)" not enough?

      What you should see

      θ = π (180°). arctan(0/−2) = arctan 0 = 0, which points the wrong way. arctan only returns angles in quadrants I and IV, so a point with a negative real part needs π added.

    Worked example

    Write the point (−3, 3) in polar coordinates in two different ways.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Plot it. x = −3, y = 3: quadrant II.
    2. Distance. r = √((−3)² + 3²) = √18 = 3√2 ≈ 4.243.
    3. Angle. tan θ = 3/(−3) = −1. The quadrant II angle with tan θ = −1 is θ = 3π/4. (−π/4 also has tangent −1, but points into quadrant IV.) So the point is (3√2, 3π/4).
    4. A second name. Walk backwards along the opposite ray: (−3√2, 3π/4 − π) = (−3√2, −π/4). Check: x = −3√2 cos(−π/4) = −3 and y = −3√2 sin(−π/4) = 3.

    Worked example 2: a plane on the radar screen

    An air-traffic radar shows a small plane 12 km from the station at θ = 210°, measured counterclockwise from due east. How far east or west, and how far north or south, is the plane?

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. The polar point. r = 12 km, θ = 210° = 7π/6: quadrant III, reference angle 30°.
    2. East–west. x = 12 cos 210° = 12 × (−√3/2) = −6√3 ≈ −10.39 km.
    3. North–south. y = 12 sin 210° = 12 × (−1/2) = −6 km.
    4. Answer. The plane is about 10.4 km west and 6 km south of the station. Check: √(10.39² + 6²) ≈ 12. Note that real navigation measures bearings clockwise from north; this problem uses the math convention.

    Common mistakes

    • Using θ = arctan(y/x) without checking the quadrant. For (−3, 3) the calculator gives −π/4, but the point is at 3π/4.
    • Thinking (r, θ) names a point uniquely. (r, θ), (r, θ + 2π) and (−r, θ + π) are all the same point.
    • Swapping sine and cosine: x goes with cos, y with sin.
    • Plotting a negative r on the ray θ. It goes on the opposite ray, θ + π.
    • Mixing degrees and radians within one problem.

    Converting equations

    The same substitutions turn a polar equation into a rectangular one. For r = 4 cos θ, multiply by r: r² = 4r cos θ, so x² + y² = 4x, which is (x − 2)² + y² = 4: a circle of radius 2 centered at (2, 0). Going the other way, the line y = 3 is r sin θ = 3, or r = 3 csc θ.

    Check yourself: Which rectangular point is the same as the polar point (−2, π/2)?

    Check yourself: Which polar form equals the complex number −1 + i?

    AP Unit 3On the AP examCED 3.14

    Polar graphs

    Give a radius for every angle and a curve draws itself: roses, hearts, loops and spirals, all from one rule r = f(θ).

    The idea

    A polar function r = f(θ) sweeps a ray around the origin and, at each angle, puts a point at distance f(θ). Sweep θ from 0 to 2π and the points trace a curve. When f(θ) is negative, the point goes on the opposite ray.

    The same function has two pictures. In the (θ, r) plane it is an ordinary graph: θ across, r up. In the polar plane it wraps around the origin. Reading one from the other is the key skill: where the rectangular graph crosses zero, the polar curve passes through the origin; where |r| peaks, the polar curve is farthest out.

    Families to know: circles r = a, r = a cos θ, r = a sin θ; roses r = a cos(nθ) with n petals if n is odd and 2n if n is even; limaçons r = a + b cos θ (inner loop if |a| < |b|, cardioid if |a| = |b|, dimpled if |b| < |a| < 2|b|, convex if |a| ≥ 2|b|); spirals r = aθ.

    Assumption upgrade

    Before
    a graph was y as a function of x, read left to right
    So we didn't need
    curves that wrap around, cross themselves or pass through the origin many times
    Now
    r = f(θ) describes shapes that are awkward or impossible as y = f(x)
    So we need
    to sweep the angle, read r from a (θ, r) graph, and handle negative r

    Two pictures, one function: 10 curves

    Read the left graph (θ across, r up), predict the polar shape, then check.

    1. This is the graph of r = 3 cos(2θ) in the (θ, r) plane. What does the polar graph look like?

    cos(nθ) with n = 2 (even) gives 2n = 4 petals. On the left graph, r hits ±3 four times per turn: each hump, up or down, is a petal.

    2. This is the graph of r = 3 sin(3θ) in the (θ, r) plane. What does the polar graph look like?

    n = 3 is odd, so 3 petals. The 6 humps on the left graph come in pairs that land on the same petal: the negative ones retrace the positive ones.

    3. This is the graph of r = 2 + 2 cos θ in the (θ, r) plane. What does the polar graph look like?

    a = b = 2: r touches 0 once (at θ = π) without going negative. That single touch is the cusp of a cardioid.

    4. This is the graph of r = 1 + 2 cos θ in the (θ, r) plane. What does the polar graph look like?

    |a| < |b|: r dips below 0 between 2π/3 and 4π/3. Negative r is drawn on the opposite ray, which makes the small inner loop.

    5. This is the graph of r = 3 + cos θ in the (θ, r) plane. What does the polar graph look like?

    r stays between 2 and 4, never near 0, and a ≥ 2b (3 ≥ 2), so the curve is convex: an egg shape, no dimple.

    6. This is the graph of r = 3 + 2 sin θ in the (θ, r) plane. What does the polar graph look like?

    b < a < 2b (2 < 3 < 4): r gets fairly small (1 at θ = 3π/2) but not 0, so the bottom caves in: a dimple. Sine makes it point up and down.

    7. This is the graph of r = 4 cos θ in the (θ, r) plane. What does the polar graph look like?

    r = a cos θ is a circle of diameter 4 through the origin: x² + y² = 4x. Between π/2 and 3π/2, r < 0 retraces the same circle.

    8. This is the graph of r = 3 in the (θ, r) plane. What does the polar graph look like?

    r is the same at every angle: every point is 3 from the origin.

    9. This is the graph of r = θ/2 in the (θ, r) plane. What does the polar graph look like?

    r keeps growing with θ, so the curve winds outward: an Archimedean spiral. (On the left graph r is a straight line.)

    10. This is the graph of r = 2 sin(4θ) in the (θ, r) plane. What does the polar graph look like?

    n = 4 is even: 2n = 8 petals.

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose Rose with n = 3, press Play. How many petals, and how many times does the left graph reach ±a?

      What you should see

      Three petals, but the left graph peaks six times (three up, three down). For odd n, the negative-r humps retrace the same petals; that is why odd n gives n petals and even n gives 2n.

    2. Rose with n = 2: count the petals now.

      What you should see

      Four petals. With n even, the negative humps land on new petals between the positive ones.

    3. Choose Limaçon a + b cos θ. Set a = 1, b = 2, then a = 2, b = 2, then a = 3, b = 2. Name each shape.

      What you should see

      a = 1: inner loop (r goes negative). a = 2: cardioid (r touches 0 once, a cusp). a = 3: dimpled limaçon (r never reaches 0, but dips to 1).

    4. Limaçon, a = 1, b = 2. Sweep θ slowly from 100° to 260° (about 1.75 to 4.5). Where is the point drawn while r is negative?

      What you should see

      On the opposite ray: at θ = π, r = −1 and the point is at (1, 0), on the right. That piece is the inner loop, drawn in magenta.

    5. In the second lab choose Circle, then drag one dot down below the θ-axis. What happens on the right?

      What you should see

      The curve dives through the origin and the point for that angle appears on the opposite side. Every zero crossing on the left is a pass through the origin on the right.

    Worked example

    Sketch r = 2 + 4 cos θ for 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π. Where does it pass through the origin, and what is the inner loop?

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Table of key angles. θ = 0, π/3, π/2, 2π/3, π give r = 6, 4, 2, 0, −2.
    2. Zeros. 2 + 4 cos θ = 0 when cos θ = −1/2: θ = 2π/3 and 4π/3. The curve passes through the origin at both angles.
    3. Negative r. For 2π/3 < θ < 4π/3, r < 0, so those points go on the opposite ray. At θ = π, r = −2 is plotted at (2, 0): this stretch makes the inner loop.
    4. Symmetry and shape. cos(−θ) = cos θ, so the curve is symmetric about the x-axis. |a| = 2 < |b| = 4: a limaçon with an inner loop, reaching out to (6, 0).

    Worked example 2: a microphone's pickup pattern

    A cardioid microphone picks up sound with relative sensitivity r = 1 + cos θ, where θ is the angle from the direction the microphone points. (a) Compare its sensitivity at the front, the side (θ = π/2) and the back. (b) At what angle is it 1.5, three-quarters of its maximum?

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Front. θ = 0: r = 1 + 1 = 2, the maximum.
    2. Side. θ = π/2: r = 1 + 0 = 1, half the front value. Half the amplitude is 20 log₁₀(0.5) ≈ −6 dB, the "−6 dB at the side" printed on microphone spec sheets.
    3. Back. θ = π: r = 1 − 1 = 0. It hears nothing from directly behind, which is why singers point it at their mouth and away from the speakers.
    4. (b) 1 + cos θ = 1.5 gives cos θ = 0.5, so θ = π/3 (60°) on either side of the front.

    Common mistakes

    • Plotting a negative r on the ray θ itself instead of the opposite ray.
    • Counting petals of r = a cos(nθ) as n for every n: it is 2n when n is even.
    • Stopping at θ = π. Many curves need the full 0 to 2π (a rose with even n, any limaçon).
    • Reading the (θ, r) graph as if it were the shape. It is a different picture of the same function.
    • Assuming every limaçon has a loop: only |a| < |b| does.

    Reading the (θ, r) graph

    AP questions often show r = f(θ) on rectangular axes and ask about the polar curve. Three translations do most of the work: r = 0 on the graph means the curve is at the origin; |r| largest means the curve is farthest out; r negative means the point is on the opposite side of the origin from the angle θ.

    Check yourself: How many petals does r = 5 sin(6θ) have?

    Check yourself: For r = 3 − 3 sin θ, at which angle does the curve pass through the origin?

    AP Unit 3On the AP examCED 3.15

    Rates of change in polar

    As θ turns, does the curve move toward the origin or away from it, and how fast? The answer is in r, not in x or y.

    The idea

    For a polar function r = f(θ), the average rate of change of r on [θ₁, θ₂] is (f(θ₂) − f(θ₁)) / (θ₂ − θ₁): how much the distance to the origin changes per radian of turning, on average. It is the slope of a secant on the (θ, r) graph.

    The sign of r and the direction r is changing together decide whether the point is getting closer to or farther from the origin. The distance is |r|. If r is positive and increasing, or negative and decreasing, |r| grows: farther. If r is positive and decreasing, or negative and increasing, |r| shrinks: closer.

    Where r changes from increasing to decreasing while positive, the curve is at a local maximum distance from the origin (the tip of a petal, the outer edge of a limaçon).

    Assumption upgrade

    Before
    rate of change was about y and x
    So we didn't need
    a rate of the distance from the origin per angle
    Now
    polar curves move toward and away from the origin as θ turns
    So we need
    the average rate of change of r and the sign test for closer or farther
    (f(θ₂) − f(θ₁)) / (θ₂ − θ₁)average rate of change of r
    r > 0 and increasingfarther from origin
    r > 0 and decreasingcloser
    r < 0 and decreasingfarther (|r| grows)
    r < 0 and increasingcloser
    Closer or farther?
    Curve
    r(θ₁) → r(θ₂)—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. With r = 1 + 2 sin θ, set θ₁ = π/2 and Δθ = 2π/3 (θ₂ = 7π/6). Compute the average rate of change, then read it.

      What you should see

      r goes from 3 to 0, so (0 − 3)/(2π/3) = −9/(2π) ≈ −1.43. r is positive and decreasing the whole way, so the point moves closer to the origin, reaching it at 7π/6.

    2. Now shrink Δθ toward 0.02 while θ₁ stays at π/2. What happens to the average rate?

      What you should see

      It approaches 0: at θ = π/2 the (θ, r) graph is at its peak, so r is momentarily neither increasing nor decreasing. The polar point is at its farthest from the origin.

    3. Choose r = 3 cos(2θ). Set θ₁ = π/4 (0.785) and Δθ = π/4. Is r positive? Is the point getting closer or farther?

      What you should see

      r goes from 0 to −3: negative and decreasing. |r| grows from 0 to 3, so the point moves farther from the origin, tracing a petal on the opposite side.

    4. Choose the sprinkler r = 10 + 4 cos θ. Compare the average rate of change on [0, π/2] and on [π, 3π/2].

      What you should see

      On [0, π/2]: (10 − 14)/(π/2) = −8/π ≈ −2.55 ft per radian (edge coming closer). On [π, 3π/2]: (10 − 6)/(π/2) = +8/π ≈ 2.55 (edge moving away).

    Worked example

    For r = f(θ) = 1 + 2 sin θ, find the average rate of change of r on [π/2, 7π/6], and say whether the curve is getting closer to or farther from the origin on that interval.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Endpoints. f(π/2) = 1 + 2(1) = 3 and f(7π/6) = 1 + 2(−1/2) = 0.
    2. Interval width. 7π/6 − π/2 = 7π/6 − 3π/6 = 2π/3.
    3. Average rate of change. (0 − 3)/(2π/3) = −9/(2π) ≈ −1.432: r drops about 1.43 units per radian, on average.
    4. Check the sign of r. On this interval sin θ > −1/2 (until 7π/6), so r > 0, and sin θ is decreasing, so r is decreasing.
    5. Conclusion. r is positive and decreasing, so the distance |r| shrinks: the curve gets closer to the origin, reaching it at θ = 7π/6.

    Worked example 2: how far the sprinkler reaches

    A lawn sprinkler waters a region whose edge is r = 10 + 4 cos θ feet from the sprinkler, θ in radians. (a) Find the average rate of change of r on [0, π/2] and interpret it. (b) Is the edge getting closer or farther on [π, 3π/2]?

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Endpoints. r(0) = 10 + 4 = 14 ft; r(π/2) = 10 + 0 = 10 ft.
    2. (a) Rate. (10 − 14)/(π/2 − 0) = −4/(π/2) = −8/π ≈ −2.546 ft per radian.
    3. Interpretation. As the spray direction turns from θ = 0 to θ = π/2, the edge of the watered region gets closer to the sprinkler at an average of about 2.55 feet per radian of turning.
    4. (b) r(π) = 6 ft and r(3π/2) = 10 ft. r is positive and increasing, so the edge is getting farther: average rate (10 − 6)/(π/2) = 8/π ≈ +2.546 ft per radian.

    Common mistakes

    • Saying "r is decreasing, so the point gets closer" when r is negative. Then |r| is growing: it moves away.
    • Using the change in x or y instead of the change in r.
    • Forgetting the units: the rate is in units of r per radian.
    • Subtracting in one order on top and the other on the bottom.
    • Using degrees in the denominator: θ₂ − θ₁ must be in radians unless told otherwise.

    Why the sign of r matters

    The distance from the origin is |r|, not r. When r is negative, the point sits on the opposite ray at distance −r. If r goes from −1 to −3, it is decreasing, but the distance goes from 1 to 3: the point moves away. So always check two things: the sign of r and whether r is increasing or decreasing.

    Check yourself: On an interval, r = f(θ) is negative and increasing. The polar curve is

    Check yourself: For r = 4 sin θ, what is the average rate of change of r on [0, π/6]?

    Parametric functions

    Give x and y each their own clock. As t ticks, the point (x(t), y(t)) moves along a path, with a direction and a speed built in.

    The idea

    A parametric function gives both coordinates as functions of a third variable, the parameter t (often time): (x(t), y(t)). As t increases, the point traces a path in the plane, in a definite direction. The path alone does not show when the point was where; the parametric function does.

    Read it as three linked pictures: the graph of x(t), the graph of y(t), and the path. When x(t) is increasing the point moves right; when y(t) is increasing it moves up. A line segment from (x₀, y₀) to (x₁, y₁) is x = x₀ + (x₁ − x₀)t, y = y₀ + (y₁ − y₀)t for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1. A circle of radius r centered at (h, k) is x = h + r cos t, y = k + r sin t, counterclockwise.

    Sometimes you can eliminate the parameter: solve one equation for t and substitute into the other to get an equation in x and y. That gives the shape of the path, but loses the direction and the timing.

    So we didn't need
    any notion of when or in which direction
    Now
    motion in the plane: where the object is at each time, so x and y both depend on t
    So we need
    parametric functions, reading direction from x(t) and y(t), and parametrizing lines and circles

    x = x₀ + (x₁ − x₀)tsegment, 0 ≤ t ≤ 1
    y = y₀ + (y₁ − y₀)t
    x = h + r cos t, y = k + r sin tcircle, counterclockwise

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose Circle and press Play. Which way does the point go, and where is it at t = π/2?

      What you should see

      Counterclockwise, starting at (3, 0). At t = π/2 it is at (3 cos π/2, 3 sin π/2) = (0, 3), the top. x(t) is a cosine and y(t) a sine.

    2. With the circle, find a time when x(t) is decreasing and y(t) is increasing. Where is the point?

      What you should see

      For 0 < t < π/2: moving left (x decreasing) and up (y increasing), so the point is in quadrant I heading toward the top.

    3. Choose Kicked ball. Watch the dots on the x(t) graph and on the path. Why are they evenly spaced across but not up?

      What you should see

      x(t) = 18t is linear: the ball covers 18 m sideways every second. y(t) is a downward parabola: fast rise, slowing at the top, then falling faster.

    4. Choose Figure-eight. The path crosses itself at the origin. Is the point ever there twice at the same time?

      What you should see

      No: it passes through (0, 0) at t = 0 and again at t = π, at different times and heading in different directions. A path can cross itself; a parametric function just visits the same place twice.

    5. In the second lab choose Stop and go back. Where does x(t) level off, and what does the point do there?

      What you should see

      Where both graphs level off together, the point stops; where they then reverse, it retraces its path backward. The path looks like a plain segment, but the motion goes out, pauses and comes back.

    Worked example

    Parametrize the segment from A(1, 2) to B(7, −1) with 0 ≤ t ≤ 1, find the point at t = 1/3, then parametrize the trip from B back to A taking 0 ≤ t ≤ 2.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Endpoints. Start A(1, 2), end B(7, −1). The change is Δx = 6 and Δy = −3.
    2. Start plus a fraction of the change. x = 1 + 6t, y = 2 − 3t, 0 ≤ t ≤ 1. At t = 0 it is A, at t = 1 it is B.
    3. t = 1/3. x = 1 + 2 = 3, y = 2 − 1 = 1: the point (3, 1), one third of the way from A to B.
    4. Reverse in 2 units of time. Start at B and cover the change (−6, 3) at half the rate: x = 7 − 3t, y = −1 + 1.5t, 0 ≤ t ≤ 2. Same path, opposite direction, different timing.

    Worked example 2: a kicked soccer ball

    A ball is kicked from 1 m above the ground. Its position after t seconds is x(t) = 18t, y(t) = 1 + 12t − 4.9t² (meters). (a) When is the ball highest, and how high? (b) When and where does it land? (c) Eliminate t to find the shape of the path.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Read each coordinate. x(t) = 18t: 18 m per second sideways, steadily. y(t) is a quadratic opening down: up, then down.
    2. (a) The vertex of y(t) is at t = −12/(2 · (−4.9)) = 12/9.8 ≈ 1.224 s. Then y = 1 + 144/19.6 ≈ 8.35 m, at x ≈ 22.0 m.
    3. (b) Lands when y = 0: 4.9t² − 12t − 1 = 0, so t = (12 + √163.6)/9.8 ≈ 2.530 s (the other root is negative). Then x = 18(2.530) ≈ 45.5 m.
    4. (c) t = x/18, so y = 1 + 12(x/18) − 4.9(x/18)² = 1 + (2/3)x − 0.01512x²: a parabola. The equation gives the shape, but not when the ball is where.

    Common mistakes

    • Treating the path as the graph of a function of x: a path can loop, cross itself or go straight up.
    • Ignoring direction: x = cos t, y = sin t and x = sin t, y = cos t trace the same circle in opposite directions.
    • Plugging x into y(t): find t first, then use it in both coordinates.
    • Forgetting the t-interval: it decides where the path starts, stops, and how many times it is traced.
    • Assuming equal steps in t give equal distances on the path.

    One path, many parametrizations

    The path x² + y² = 1 is the circle, but (cos t, sin t), (cos 2t, sin 2t), (sin t, cos t) and (cos t, −sin t) are four different motions on it: different speeds and directions. Planar motion problems care about the motion, so the parametric function carries more information than the path.

    Check yourself: Which is a parametrization of the circle of radius 2 centered at (1, −3), counterclockwise?

    Check yourself: On an interval, x(t) is decreasing and y(t) is constant. The point is moving

    AP Unit 4 · not on examNot on the AP examCED 4.3

    Parametric rates of change

    A moving point has two rates: how fast it moves sideways and how fast it moves up. Their ratio is the slope of the path.

    The idea

    For a parametric function (x(t), y(t)), each coordinate has its own rate of change. Over an interval [t₁, t₂], the average rates are Δx/Δt = (x(t₂) − x(t₁))/(t₂ − t₁) and Δy/Δt, defined the same way. They are the horizontal and vertical speeds of the point, on average.

    The slope of the line through the two points of the path, the average rate of change of y with respect to x, is the ratio of the two: Δy/Δx = (Δy/Δt) / (Δx/Δt), as long as Δx ≠ 0. The time cancels. As the interval shrinks, these rates approach the rates at an instant, and the slope approaches the direction the point is heading.

    Signs tell direction: if x(t) is increasing on an interval, the point moves right; decreasing, left. If y(t) is increasing it moves up. Where x(t) has a turning point the path has a vertical tangent (the point momentarily moves straight up or down); where y(t) turns, a horizontal one.

    Assumption upgrade

    Before
    rate of change meant Δy/Δx for one function
    So we didn't need
    a way to talk about sideways and vertical speed separately
    Now
    a moving point has a horizontal rate and a vertical rate at the same time
    So we need
    average rates of x(t) and y(t), the slope Δy/Δx of the path, and direction from the signs
    Δx/Δt = (x(t₂) − x(t₁))/(t₂ − t₁)horizontal rate
    Δy/Δt = (y(t₂) − y(t₁))/(t₂ − t₁)vertical rate
    Δy/Δx = (Δy/Δt) / (Δx/Δt)slope of the path
    x(t) increasingmoving right
    y(t) turnshorizontal tangent

    Motion

    Which way is it moving? 6 cases

    Read the direction from x(t) and y(t) alone, then see the path.

    1. x(t) and y(t) near the marked time are shown. Which way is the point moving?

    At the marked time x(t) is decreasing (moving left) and y(t) is increasing (moving up): the point heads up and left. (x = 2 cos t, y = 2 sin t, t = 1.2)

    2. x(t) and y(t) near the marked time are shown. Which way is the point moving?

    At the marked time x(t) is decreasing (moving left) and y(t) is decreasing (moving down): the point heads down and left. (x = t² − 2t, y = 3 − t, t = 0.5)

    3. x(t) and y(t) near the marked time are shown. Which way is the point moving?

    At the marked time x(t) is increasing (moving right) and y(t) is increasing (moving up): the point heads up and right. (x = 1 + t, y = (t − 1)², t = 2.0)

    4. x(t) and y(t) near the marked time are shown. Which way is the point moving?

    At the marked time x(t) is increasing (moving right) and y(t) is decreasing (moving down): the point heads down and right. (x = 2 sin t, y = sin 2t, t = 5.3)

    5. x(t) and y(t) near the marked time are shown. Which way is the point moving?

    At the marked time x(t) is decreasing (moving left) and y(t) is decreasing (moving down): the point heads down and left. (x = 3 − t²/2, y = t² − 4t + 3, t = 1.2)

    6. x(t) and y(t) near the marked time are shown. Which way is the point moving?

    At the marked time x(t) is increasing (moving right) and y(t) is increasing (moving up): the point heads up and right. (x = t − sin t, y = 1 − cos t, t = 2.0)

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose Kicked ball with t₁ = 0 and t₂ = 1. Then move both up by 1 second. Which rate stays the same?

      What you should see

      Δx/Δt = 18 m/s on every interval: x(t) = 18t is linear. Δy/Δt drops from 7.1 to −2.7 m/s: the ball rises, then falls.

    2. Choose Runner on a track, t₁ = 0 and t₂ = 20. Why is Δx/Δt negative while the runner is going forward?

      What you should see

      Running counterclockwise from (50, 0) to (0, 50), x shrinks from 50 to 0: Δx/Δt = −2.5 m/s, moving left, even though the runner never slows down.

    3. Choose Figure-eight and set t₁ = 0, t₂ = π (3.14). What is the slope of the chord, and why?

      What you should see

      Both endpoints are the origin, so Δx = Δy = 0: no chord, the slope is undefined. Average rates of 0 do not mean the point stood still.

    4. In the second lab, choose Circle and shrink h toward 0.01. What does the chord turn into?

      What you should see

      The tangent direction: the chord rotates until it just touches the circle at the point, perpendicular to the radius.

    5. With Figure-eight, find a time where the tangent is vertical. What is x(t) doing there?

      What you should see

      At t = π/2 the point is at the right end (3, 0): x(t) = 3 sin t reaches its maximum and turns around, so Δx/Δt → 0 while y keeps changing. The path is vertical there.

    Worked example

    A ball is kicked with x(t) = 18t and y(t) = 1 + 12t − 4.9t² (meters, seconds). Find the average rates of change of x and y, and the slope of the path, on [0, 1] and on [1, 2].

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Positions. t = 0: (0, 1). t = 1: (18, 8.1). t = 2: (36, 5.4), since y(2) = 1 + 24 − 19.6 = 5.4.
    2. [0, 1]. Δx/Δt = (18 − 0)/1 = 18 m/s; Δy/Δt = (8.1 − 1)/1 = 7.1 m/s; slope Δy/Δx = 7.1/18 ≈ 0.394.
    3. [1, 2]. Δx/Δt = 18 m/s again; Δy/Δt = (5.4 − 8.1)/1 = −2.7 m/s; slope = −2.7/18 = −0.15.
    4. Read it. Same sideways speed, but the vertical rate went from positive to negative: the ball passed its highest point between t = 1 and t = 2 (at t ≈ 1.22 s).

    Worked example 2: a runner on a circular track

    A runner goes counterclockwise around a circular track of radius 50 m, centered at the origin, starting at (50, 0) and taking 80 s per lap: x(t) = 50 cos(πt/40), y(t) = 50 sin(πt/40). Find Δx/Δt and Δy/Δt on [0, 20], and compare the distance run with the straight-line distance.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Positions. t = 0: (50, 0). t = 20: πt/40 = π/2, so (0, 50), a quarter lap.
    2. Rates. Δx/Δt = (0 − 50)/20 = −2.5 m/s (moving left); Δy/Δt = (50 − 0)/20 = 2.5 m/s (moving up). The chord has slope 2.5/(−2.5) = −1.
    3. Distance run. A quarter of the circumference: 2π(50)/4 = 25π ≈ 78.54 m, at a constant 78.54/20 ≈ 3.93 m/s.
    4. Straight line. The chord is 50√2 ≈ 70.71 m, so the average rates describe a slower, straight-line trip (√(2.5² + 2.5²) ≈ 3.54 m/s). Average rates only see the endpoints.

    Common mistakes

    • Dividing Δx/Δt by Δy/Δt for the slope: it is (Δy/Δt) / (Δx/Δt), rise over run.
    • Reading a negative Δx/Δt as "slowing down": it means moving left.
    • Expecting the slope of the path to exist when Δx = 0, or that zero average rates mean no motion.
    • Using x-values instead of t-values in the denominator of Δx/Δt.

    Rates at an instant

    Shrinking the interval turns the average rates into the rates at an instant: the horizontal and vertical velocity. In calculus these are x′(t) and y′(t), and the slope of the path is dy/dx = y′(t)/x′(t). Precalculus works with average rates and with the signs (which way, and where it turns); the lab shows the limit as a picture.

    Check yourself: On [2, 5], x(t) goes from 4 to −2 and y(t) from 1 to 10. What is the average rate of change of y with respect to x?

    Check yourself: On an interval, x(t) is increasing and y(t) is decreasing. The point is moving

    Which tool do I use?

    Most of the time lost on the exam goes into choosing a model or a method. Learn the clues, then practice picking.

    The intuition

    Each problem leaves clues. Equal steps in x with equal differences in y is linear; equal ratios is exponential. Something that repeats is sinusoidal. An unknown in the exponent calls for a logarithm. A distance and an angle means polar. Name the model or method first; the algebra is the easy part.

    Exam review

    Build a mixed problem set from the units your exam covers. No hints during the set; everything is graded and explained when you submit.

    Exam format

    AP Precalculus · May 2027 exam · 2 hours 55 minutes

    Section I: Multiple choice
    42 questions · 105 min · 62.5%
    • Part A: 29 questions, 65 min, no calculator
    • Part B: 13 questions, 40 min, graphing calculator required
    Section II: Free response
    4 questions · 70 min · 37.5%
    • Part A: 2 questions, 35 min, graphing calculator required (Q1 function concepts, Q2 modeling a non-periodic context)
    • Part B: 2 questions, 35 min, no calculator (Q3 modeling a periodic context, Q4 symbolic manipulations)
    How you take it
    Hybrid digital. You answer multiple choice in the Bluebook app. Free-response questions appear in Bluebook, and you handwrite your answers in a paper booklet.
    What's tested
    Units 1–3: polynomial and rational (30–40% of multiple choice), exponential and logarithmic (25–40%), trigonometric and polar (30–35%). Unit 4 (parameters, vectors, matrices) is taught in the course but not on the exam; use Units: AP exam in the menu to hide it.
    Reference sheet
    None. You need to know the identities and rules yourself; this site's Reference button helps you learn them.
    What changed
    For May 2027, multiple choice Part A went from 28 questions in 80 minutes to 29 in 65, Part B from 12 to 13 questions, and each free-response part from 30 to 35 minutes.

    Checked October 24, 2026 against College Board's published format. Formats can change, so confirm on AP Central before your exam.

    Review my mistakes

    Every problem you miss in the practice set or exam review lands here and comes back with new numbers. Spacing reviews out over days is one of the most reliable ways to make things stick.

    How the queue works

    Miss a problem: it's due right away. Get it right: it comes back in 1 day, then 3 days, then 7. After three correct reviews in a row it's mastered and leaves the queue. Miss it again and the count restarts.
